call: This funding organization is dedicated to catalyzing multidisciplinary scientific teams to synthesize publicly available data to address fundamental questions related to emergence phenomena in the molecular and cellular biosciences. It supports community-scale synthesis and integration of existing molecular and cellular data to: Answer novel questions Solve long-standing puzzles in the molecular and cellular sciences Develop innovative research and analytical strategies Tap diverse new talent Train the future data-savvy workforce A community-scale synthesis project has three defining characteristics. First, it uses only existing publicly available data and often integrates distinct datasets together. It does not generate any new experimental data. Second, the project is beyond the capabilities of most individual research labs and instead requires collaboration between two or more labs. Finally, such a project requires diverse scientific perspectives and expertise to come together, often resulting in novel, deeper, and broader insights. You research should focus on well-defined scientific questions or methodological developments that advance molecular and cellular sciences through synthesis research to acquire insights from a collaborative, transdisciplinary approach. This RFP invites proposals for Working Groups that will: Address Compelling Scientific Questions: Tackle novel and significant research questions in molecular and cellular biology through data synthesis. Stimulate Cross-Disciplinary Collaboration: Bring together researchers from diverse fields. Utilize Publicly Available Data: Leverage existing data sources to develop innovative research and analytical strategies. Require NCEMS Support and Resources: The proposed synthesis project must demonstrate a clear need for NCEMS support that goes beyond the capabilities of a single lab or existing collaboration. Promote Collaborative Partnerships: Assemble teams that reflect a range of scientific expertise, geographic locations, career stages, and institutional research levels. Adhere to Open Science Principles: Commit to making findings, data, and analysis workflows publicly available in accordance with community-created policies on open, team, and reproducible science. Train the Next Generation: Provide training opportunities to trainees (graduate students and postdocs) through collaborative research efforts within the working group.

proposals.abstract: The lack of motility makes plants highly vulnerable to environmental anomalies such as periods of extreme high temperature known as heat waves. Plants can search for better habitats by exploiting seed mobility, which relies on completing the life cycle and producing seeds. Formation of reproductive organs and seed development requires the production of cells through cell division. The last stage of cell division, cytokinesis, encompasses many key cellular processes, including vesicle trafficking, cell wall biosynthesis, cytoskeletal dynamics, and signaling. While cytokinesis is highly sensitive to heat stress in plants adapted to temperate climates, cytokinesis is more resilient in species adapted to tropical zones. However, how heat stress affects cytokinesis and the mechanisms of cytokinetic robustness across different plant species remains unknown. This project aims to compare changes in cytokinetic components under heat stress in susceptible and hardy species to characterize differential responses of genetic circuits responsible for specific cellular events during cytokinesis. The long term goal is to harness this data for identifying the bottlenecks of cytokinetic robustness. The experimental approach here will be systematic analysis of publicly available data from single-cell and whole-organ omics data collected under control and high-temperature conditions including transcriptomics, translatomics, and proteomics. Predicting cytokinetic bottlenecks will inform future experimental design for their functional characterization leading to better understanding of cellular adaptation mechanisms to heat stress. This knowledge may provide insight into evolutionary strategies of plant adaptation to different climates and improve predictions for heat resiliency at the level of individual plants and populations.

4. Introduction 4.1. Problem overview. 4.1.1. Cytokinesis is critical for plant life. The majority of planetary plant biomass derives from cytokinesis1. Plant cytokinesis occurs via the formation of a specialized membrane compartment, the cell plate, between daughter cells. The cell plate gradually matures into a cell wall after cytokinesis is complete. One of the key processes accompanying this transition is replacing callose, the main polysaccharide in the cell plate lumen, with cellulose. A plant-specific polarized secretory module, the phragmoplast, is responsible for constructing the cell plate (Figure 1A). The phragmoplast consists of microtubules and actin cytoskeleton, vesicles, and associated proteins. As the phragmoplast diameter is commonly smaller than the cell width, completing the cell plate construction requires phragmoplast expansion (Figure 1B). The expansion is driven by microtubules and requires coordination between microtubule dynamics, membrane and cell-wall-component trafficking, exocytosis, vesicle fusion, and endocytosis2-6. Phragmoplast expansion encompasses four steps: (1) establishment of microtubule overlap, (2) vesicle recruitment, (3) vesicle fusion and remodeling, and (4) microtubule depolymerization (Figure 1C)3. Each step requires a dedicated genetic network comprising structural proteins, enzymes, and signaling components. 4.1.2. Cytokinesis is sensitive to heat stress. Exposing tobacco tissue culture cells to 38°C for 2 h causes cytokinetic arrest and elongation of phragmoplast microtubules7 while cells remain viable; subsequently, microtubule organization does not recover even by 2 hours at normal temperature, indicating that the arrest is long-term. In meiotic Arabidopsis cells treated at 36-38°C, chromosome segregation is disrupted and microtubule density in the phragmoplast is reduced8. In the flowering sea grass, Cymodocea nodosa, treatment at 38°C for 2 h depolymerizes some phragmoplast microtubules9 but does not block Figure 1. Phragmoplast structure and expansion. A, The phragmoplast forms between daughter nuclei (Disk stage). The cell plate synthesis takes place in the midzone. Microtubules function as a scaffold. Cytokinetic vesicles are guided by microtubules to the midzone where they fuse and undergo remodeling to form tubule-vesicular network. Cell plate lumen becomes filled with callose. B, Once the cell plate in disk phragmoplast becomes rigid, the expansion starts through microtubule depolymerization and polymerization of freed tubulin at the cell plate edge (Ring stage). The expansion continues until the cell plate connects with the plasma membrane at which point the phragmoplast vanishes. C, Phragmoplast expansion starts with MAP65 and kinesins establishing microtubule overlap at the midzone (Step 1). The overlap recruits cytokinetic vesicles through interaction with tethering factors such as TRAPPII in Step 2. At Step 3 cytokinetic vesicles fuse and undergo remodeling while the microtubule overlap dissolve and microtubules attach to the membrane. At Step 4 microtubules become unnecessary and depolymerize. cytokinesis. The graded heat stress responses among species will allow us to identify both common and distinct resilience mechanisms of cytokinesis. 4.1.3. Outcomes of prior studies 4.1.3.1. Cytokinesis is differentially sensitive to heat stress within the plant lineage. Arabidopsis plants are killed at ~35ºC whereas maize plants are killed by temperatures at least 10 degrees higher 10,11 . Consequently, maize cytokinesis could be resilient to heat stress. We compared the impact of heat stress on cytokinesis in these species. On the basis of published data 38°C was used to induce stress. Exposure of 6-day old Arabidopsis seedlings to 38°C for 1 hour caused cell plate tilting and disorganization, as indicated by the cytokinetic vesicle marker RABA2a (Figure 2A). Cell plate assembly failed resulting in formation of cell wall stubs (Figure 2B) and phragmoplasts were aberrantly long (Figure 2B, C). We examined microtubule stability in the elongated phragmoplasts using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) and found very slow recovery of the fluorescent signal (Figure 2D). As the signal recovery requires microtubule depolymerization, this outcome suggests that heat stress suppressed depolymerization of phragmoplast microtubules. Oppositely, in 3-week old maize seedlings the phragmoplast morphology appeared unaltered and no cell wall stubs were detected even after exposure to 42°C or 45°C (Figure 2E, F). Thus, cytokinesis is heat-resilient in maize. This outcome is consistent with the USDA report that the 2021 heat wave caused yield losses to all dryland farming crops except maize 12 . Therefore, comparing the impact of 38°C on cytokinetic components in Arabidopsis and tobacco with those in maize will likely inform on mechanisms of cytokinetic robustness. 4.1.3.2. Impact of heat stress on transcription and translation of cytokinetic genes. While analyzing the impact of heat stress on circadian clock-regulated genes 13 (Figure 3A), we discovered changes in both the abundance of mRNAs and in the ribosome-binding (or actively translated) fraction, encoding key cytokinetic genes. For example, the phragmoplast-localized kinesin HINKEL 14,15 was reduced after heat treatment on both transcriptome and translatome levels (Figure 3B). AIR9 16,17 transcripts were not significantly affected by heat treatment (Figure 3C). Heat stress resulted in lower transcription and translation of 11 cytokinetic genes with the exception of midzone localized formin homology protein for AtFH8 18 whose translation was specifically upregulated (Figure 3D). AtFH8 might contribute to the stabilization of microtubule plus-ends at the phragmoplast midzone 19 . Up-regulation of this protein could be a mechanism to sustain phragmoplast organization under heat stress. Therefore, comparison of transcriptome and translatome data captures the complexity of cytokinetic gene regulation in responses to stresses 13,20 . 4.1.4. Conceptual framework. According to the theory of biological robustness, genetic networks for individual traits contain specific robustness alleles instead of a master robustness allele acting across multiple networks 21 . Consequently, known robustness alleles for other traits are unlikely to contribute to heat resiliency of cytokinesis. Instead, cytokinetic robustness must be achieved by temporally controlling and genetically buffering distinct cytokinetic processes in a modular fashion. When a genetic network experiences an interruption, both the central hubs and less connected nodes could either limit or maintain resiliency. Consequently, identifying cytokinetic bottlenecks requires generating cytokinetic protein networks and comparing their behaviour under normal and stress conditions. Construction of cytokinetic networks is hindered by limited information about their components. Despite genetic screens for cytokinetic mutants have already identified multiple players 14,22-25 , many cytokinetic genes remain unidentified either due to genetic redundancy or lethality. Furthermore, despite biophysical modeling indicating that callose provides the spreading force for membrane remodeling during cell plate expansion 26 , there are numerous knowledge gaps about other carbohydrates and corresponding enzymes during cytokinesis. 4.2. Goals. The long-term goal of our research is to determine the rules and limits of cytokinetic robustness under heat stress and harness this knowledge for improving plant resiliency. Although it has been shown that high temperatures perturb membrane assembly and cytoskeletal dynamics during cytokinesis the underlying molecular mechanisms of such changes remain unknown. The objective of this project is to exploit available data to predict bottlenecks of cytokinesis. A bottleneck is defined as a gene whose product becomes dysfunction-al or less functional in response to heat stress. The rationale for this project is based on the following elements: (i) heat stress indices transcriptional changes of genes encoding cytokinetic proteins; (ii) plants adapted to hotter environments likely evolved mechanisms to buffer the effects of heat stress on cell division; (iii) analysis of available data can inform on differences of cytokinetic responses in heat resilient and heat tolerant species. We plan to achieve the main objective through three specific aims below. 5. Proposed Activities. 5.1. Aim#1. Construct cytokinetic networks using single-cell omics data. Our knowledge about cytokinetic components is limited to several dozens of cytokinesis-defective mutants, a few protein-protein interaction maps, and information about mitotic transcripts. Many proteins required for cytokinesis remain unknown. This aim will take a holistic approach to identify the cytokinetic gene networks using single-cell transcriptomics data from plant species including A.thaliana, Z. mays, O. sativa, S. bicolor, and N. tabacum to identify conserved cytokinetic transcripts, as well as species-specific cytokinetic transcripts. Raw data will be reprocessed following a standardized pipeline for all omics datasets to allow for effective comparative analysis and interpretation of the data. For single-cell transcriptomics, the analysis for count normalization, dimensionality reduction, clustering visualization, trajectory analysis, and differential gene expression analysis may vary depending on the lab. Therefore, data reprocessing will account for variation and enable statistically significant perturbations to be compared. Then the following pipeline will be used. First, a list of mitotic-related genes including paralogs will be compiled for Arabidopsis from published data. Second, a standardized pipeline such as OrthoFinder27 will identify orthologous genes from maize, sorghum, rice, and tobacco. Third, the single-cell transcriptome data (see Table 12) will be either analyzed or reanalyzed to identify co-expressed transcripts. Fourth, transcripts that are only expressed in cells expressing known mitotic-specific transcripts will be selected as benchmark transcripts to identify coexpressing transcripts. Then, transcripts that appear in < 50% of the datasets per organism will be more closely assessed for removal from the list. The expected outcome would be a table of Arabidopsis mitosis/cytokinesis proteins and their homologs in other plant species. 5.2. Aim#2. Compare cytokinetic responses to heat stress in heat susceptible and resilient species. Our preliminary experiments demonstrate that cytokinesis is heat-sensitive in tobacco and A. thaliana, and heat-tolerant in Z. mays. This aim will compare omics data of Z. mays and other heat-tolerant species with those of heat-sensitive species. As in Aim#1, the raw data will be reprocessed. Analysis will focus on identifying responses that are different between tolerance and susceptible species for each type of omics analyses. We will also identify the transcription factors and cis-regulatory components of these genes that act specifically in heat stress response using available ChIP-seq data28. Completing this aim will inform on which pathways are affected by heat stress in heat tolerant and susceptible species. 5.3. Aim#3. Predict cytokinetic bottlenecks through integration of available datasets. The activities in this aim will construct multi-layered cytokinetic-specific networks and compare their changes under heat stress conditions in susceptible and tolerant species. The first step will be single-layer analysis within a single type (or layer) of omics data. Analyses for each layer will include: differential analysis, correlation network analysis, time series clustering, and association networks. The second stage will be construction of a multiplex network that combines single-layer networks from different omics datasets into a multilayer model. Connections, or edges, between the layers indicate inter-layer relationships. Analysis of networks is expected to generate candidate molecular features with potential influence on differences in cytokinetic responses. These comparisons are predicted to identify cytokinetic bottlenecks under heat stress. We will write a manuscript on this topic and submit it towards the end of year 2. 5.4. Potential problems could arise from the datasets being generated using plants grown under different conditions as well as due to the differences in how the normalization and further analysis were performed. To address this problem we will reanalyze all datasets as outlined in Specific Aim 1, and also including a large number of datasets will help to average the noise caused by variable growth conditions. 6. Outcomes. We anticipate this project will predict cytokinetic bottlenecks under heat stress. This information will be used to formulate the theory of cytokinetic responses to heat stress. The theory will aim to answer the following questions. Which changes to cytokinetic processes in response to heat stress measured either at the transcript or the protein level are common to all species or species-specific? Are there specific subsets of cytokinesis genes or paralogs that have a differential response to heat stress? Do plants eliminate proteins/transcripts or stabilize them to adapt to heat stress? Would these changes promote or block cytokinesis? We will publish this theory as a review article. The theory will inform on the experiments that will lead to the identification of novel genetic, biochemical and cellular markers of plant heat stress response. Such markers would enable: (i) predicting the performance of individual species and stability of entire ecosystems under elevated temperatures; (ii) identifying resilient genotypes among the available germplasm for urban ecosystems and afforestation projects; (iii) breeding crops with higher yield in hotter environments; (iv) developing new approaches for engineering heat-resilient landscaping plant species to contribute to sustainable habitats for humans and animals. 7. Rationale for a working group approach. Our team possesses expertise in cell biology of plant cytokinesis (Rasmussen), membrane trafficking (Drakakaki), heat stress impact on plant physiology (Nagel), and protein biochemistry (Smertenko). We collectively have a deep mechanistic understanding of cytokinesis. Further, we collected preliminary data showing that heat stress does not break cytokinetic processes in susceptible plant species, but prevents cytokinetic progression through the arrest of cellular dynamics. The next logical step is to identify cytokinetic pathways affected by the heat stress, and compare them in tolerant and susceptible species using a bioinformatics approach. We want to team up with NCEMS for the next important stage in understanding the impact of heat stress on cytokinesis. 8. Rationale for NCEMS support. We hope to gain access to professional expertise in bioinformatics and complex data analysis available at NCEMS. Publicly available single-cell and whole-tissue heat stress omics data offers rich material for predicting cytokinetic bottlenecks. Collaboration with NCEMS scientists will lower the barriers of analyzing publicly available omics data for PIs Smertenko, Rasmussen, Nagel, and Drakakaki. Our cell biological data suggests that there will be differentially regulated cytokinetic pathways in heat tolerant and susceptible organisms and we can predict them using bioinformatics analyses. There is currently no alternative funding mechanism to support the transition from an initial concept to an experimental analysis. This project will contribute to developing the theory of cytokinetic robustness and help us to design experiments to test it. 9. Requested resources. To successfully perform the work described in the Aims above, a Staff scientist with bioinformatics expertise is requested for 4 months per year and an Assistant Staff Scientist (graduate student) for 6 months per year for 2 years. Computational resources for storage and data processing are also needed to successfully implement and achieve the above Aims. To accommodate the download and storage of the publically available datasets listed in item 12 (Data Sources Table) and support the analyses we estimate and are requesting 50 TB of storage and 25,000 CPU hours. 10. proposals.proposal_title: Elucidating genome structure-function relationships in human brain cells
proposals.abstract: Single-cell analysis has profoundly enhanced our understanding of brain tissue by facilitating the examination of gene expression and epigenetic features. However, investigating these modalities independently offers a fragmented view of gene regulation and its relationship to transcriptional activity. To overcome this limitation, we propose developing a multimodal generative AI model that integrates single-cell genomics datasets. This framework seeks to illuminate the interplay between three-dimensional genomic architecture and gene expression, uncovering the physical principles underlying the emergence of cell-type-specific gene expression programs, despite the inherent stochasticity of gene regulation at the single-cell level. Applied to datasets from Alzheimer's patients, this approach has the potential to identify epigenetic drivers of disease progression, thereby contributing to a deeper understanding of neurodegenerative processes.
proposals.full_draft: Introduction and Goals The human brain is a highly complex biological system that contains a wide array of distinct cell types, each characterized by specific functions and properties. Understanding this intricate neural architecture requires an investigation into the molecular mechanisms that regulate the brain's cellular diversity, development, and function. A key aspect of this research is the classification of all cell types and the elucidation of their origins from a shared genetic framework. All brain cells share the same genome, yet their identities and functions are shaped by their epigenomes, which consist of covalent modifications to histones and DNA. Chromatin, the structure formed by DNA wrapping around histone proteins, regulates gene expression in eukaryotic cells through a complex network of chemical modifications. These modifications determine the transcriptional activity of the genome within each cell, thus defining their distinct characteristics and roles. To fully characterize a cell, it is essential to identify specific chemical modifications in DNA regions, assess DNA accessibility, analyze chromatin spatial organization, and measure RNA transcription. Single-cell analysis provides a powerful framework for uncovering details and variability often obscured in population-averaged studies. By profiling RNA expression1,2, chromatin accessibility3, chromatin organization4, and DNA methylation4, such analyses have advanced our understanding of the cellular diversity within human brain tissue, shedding light on the intricate epigenetic elements that may constitute regulatory networks. Nonetheless, examining individual modalities at the single-cell level offers an incomplete perspective on the complexity of gene regulatory networks and is insufficient for inferring causal relationships between these networks and gene expression. We propose methodologies to integrate single-cell genomics data for constructing multimodal datasets. With these datasets, we will develop a multimodal generative AI (artificial intelligence) model to capture the distribution across three genomic domains: chromatin accessibility, three-dimensional (3D) chromatin organization, and gene expression. This model will define genomic states, offering molecular insights into neuron characteristics, and facilitate a mechanistic understanding of the structure-function relationships within the genome. Further applying the model to single-cell data collected from Alzheimer’s patients will provide insight into molecular determinants that drive disease progression. Proposed Activities Develop a multimodal model for human brain cells. A primary objective of the working group is to develop a multimodal model that integrates chromatin accessibility and 3D chromatin organization with gene expression. This initiative is inspired by recent advances in deep learning techniques, particularly in AI models capable of synthesizing text and image data to provide comprehensive contextual insights5–8. These models have shown considerable effectiveness across various domains, including multimodal data analysis and predictive modeling 9–11. The development of this model will enhance the understanding of chromatin organization’s functional role in regulating gene expression under normal conditions and its potential contribution to aberrant gene expression during disease progression. Model Design. The proposed model is based on the transformer architecture12, linking DNA sequences and chromatin accessibility to gene expression (Figure 1A). The design builds upon the framework of EPCOT introduced by Zhang et al. 13, which generates transferable embeddings for DNA sequence and chromatin accessibility data that can be fine-tuned for diverse downstream tasks. Notably, Zhang et al. demonstrated that these embeddings enable reliable predictions of gene expression from bulk RNA-seq data. Our approach introduces two key advances: a focus on single-cell RNA-seq prediction and the incorporation of structural information from single-cell Hi-C data to improve predictive accuracy. Figure 1. Architecture of the proposed deep learning models for integrating and analyzing various modality of single cell data. (A) Aligning the embedding of single-cell RNA-seq (function) and Hi-C (structure) produced by two encoders (scGPT and vision transformer) using contrastive learning. (B) Predicting single-cell RNA-seq using a multimodal model with both DNA sequence (+ chromatin accessibility) and single-cell Hi-C as input. The 3D chromatin organization captured by single-cell Hi-C is represented as a contact matrix and processed using the established Vision Transformer architecture16, originally designed for image data but has shown great success in analyzing Hi-C data14. The Vision Transformer encoder transforms the 3D chromatin data into numerical embeddings, which are integrated into the expression prediction module through cross-attention layers. Specifically, the 3D organization is represented by a 20-MB contact matrix centered on the target gene at a resolution of 5 kb. This matrix encapsulates the structural context surrounding the gene, including chromatin loops, topologically associating domains (TADs), and compartments. Importantly, the spatial range of the proposed model substantially exceeds that of existing approaches incorporating structural data for gene expression prediction15–18, which are typically limited to a 1-MB scale. The broader coverage and multiscale structural features enable the model to capture a diverse array of gene regulatory mechanisms. Model Parameterization and Validation. Parameterizing this model requires co-assay data obtained from experiments that concurrently measure chromatin organization and gene expression19–23. Due to the limited availability of such datasets, which exist only for a small number of cell types, we propose adopting a pretraining and fine-tuning approach to enhance the model's transferability. The encoder for single-cell Hi-C will be pretrained using data sources 1 and 2, which provide chromatin organization and gene expression information at single-cell resolution for various human brain tissue. These datasets have been consolidated into a consensus list of cell types, facilitating the learning of cell-type-specific chromatin organization features that underpin the corresponding gene expression programs. Beyond generating embeddings for gene expression prediction, the proposed model, termed scCOE (single-cell chromatin organization embedding), is expected to serve as a robust tool for extracting interpretable features of chromatin organization. Our pretraining strategy is inspired by the method employed in CLIP 24, a computational framework developed by OpenAI that achieves co-embedding of text and image data, thereby linking two distinct modalities. Specifically, we will utilize contrastive learning to align embeddings for chromatin organization with embeddings for gene expression derived from scGPT (Figure 1B). scGPT, a large language model trained on single-cell RNA-seq data from 33 million cells25, has demonstrated significant utility in biologically meaningful tasks, including cell type annotation, perturbation response prediction, and gene network inference. By aligning chromatin organization embeddings with those from scGPT, our approach aims to uncover structurally relevant features linked to gene function. During this phase, gene expression embeddings will be precomputed and held constant, while only the parameters of the vision transformer encoding chromatin organization will be optimized. A critical advantage of using contrastive learning lies in its ability to optimize the model using single-cell data derived from separate experiments. Although chromatin organization and gene expression are not measured in the same cells in sources 2 and 3, their categorization into a consensus set of cell types allows model optimization. In particular, within the framework of contrastive learning, it is straightforward to optimize the embeddings such that chromatin organization and gene expression from the same cell type share higher similarity than those from different cell types. Following pretraining, the complete model, named scGEP (single-cell gene expression prediction), will be fine-tuned using data sources 3 and 4. Source 3 leverages a novel co-assay technique, invented by co-lead Longzhi Tan, to simultaneously profile genome organization and gene expression for GM12878 cells. Unfortunately, co-assay data for human brain cells are unavailable. Nevertheless, assuming that different cell types share similar gene regulatory mechanisms, we anticipate that the model fine-tuned with GM12878 cells will be transferable to brain cells. Chromatin accessibility is assessed at the bulk level via ATAC-seq. At this stage, the chromatin organization and DNA sequence + ATAC-seq encoders will be directly adopted from the pretrained EPCOT model, with their parameters frozen. Training will focus on the green module of the model in Figure 1A, designed to predict single-cell gene expression based on single-cell chromatin organization, contextualized by bulk chromatin accessibility. Tensor decomposition. After preparing the data for our AI model, we can enhance our analysis by performing tensor decomposition26 on this data, a technique successfully applied in projects like the COVID-19 Multi-Omics Blood Atlas28 and Genomic Advances in Sepsis (GAinS)27. This supplementary analysis offers two key benefits: 1. Dimensionality Reduction and Outlier Detection: By decomposing our multi-modal data into components, we can reduce its dimensionality, providing a clearer understanding of its structure. This process enhances our ability to identify, and if necessary, remove outliers that could adversely affect our primary analysis. 2. Handling Missing Data through Imputation: The proposed tensor decomposition method26 is capable of accommodating missing data, making it ideal for samples lacking information in certain modalities that we still wish to include. By reconstructing the data from the decomposed tensors, we can impute these missing values, potentially expanding our dataset and enriching our main analysis. Potential Caveats. We will adhere to the standard practice of dividing the data into training, validation, and testing subsets to assess the performance of the resulting models. The limited availability of co-assay data may impact the transferability of the resulting model. If upon evaluation, we find that the model’s performance is not satisfactory, additional training will be carried out using co-assay data from sources 7 and 8. While these data are primarily for mouse cells and sequencing depth is not as extensive as source 3, they may serve as useful data for model pretraining. Hypothesis 1: Variation in genome organization drives gene expression changes. Despite extensive efforts, the precise mechanisms governing gene expression remain poorly understood. Previous studies have reported conflicting conclusions regarding the significance of chromatin organization in regulating gene expression. These inconsistencies often arise because such investigations have either focused on a limited set of genes or relied on population-averaged data. The availability of genome-wide datasets, encompassing both the expression of all genes and their corresponding 3D organization from the same cell, provides an opportunity for systematic exploration of chromatin's role in gene regulation. Primary Question: The computational tool proposed here, scCOE, offers a framework to associate changes in chromatin organization with variations in gene expression. Traditional analyses have emphasized structural motifs, such as chromatin loops, TADs, and compartments, but the functional relevance and specific contributions of these features remain uncertain. scCOE generates embeddings optimized to align with gene expression, capturing functionally significant structural characteristics. Investigating the variation of these embeddings across human brain cell types can provide valuable insights into the role of chromatin organization in the generation of neuronal diversity from the same DNA sequence. Furthermore, this approach enables the examination of how heterogeneity in gene expression within a single cell type correlates with variations in chromatin architecture. Secondary Question: While scCOE offers qualitative insights into the influence of chromatin organization on gene expression, the computational tool scGEP quantitatively assesses whether chromatin organization is sufficient for accurate expression prediction. The multimodal model's performance will be compared to models incorporating only DNA sequence, chromatin accessibility, or chromatin organization. We hypothesize that a model based solely on DNA sequence will perform moderately well but lack precision. Adding chromatin organization as a contextual feature is expected to substantially improve predictions of cell type-specific gene expression patterns. Hypothesis 2: Functionally relevant embedding of genome organization offers insight into Alzheimer’s disease. Genome organization is hierarchical, encoding vast amounts of information. Interpreting changes within this organization, particularly in normal versus diseased cells, poses significant challenges. For instance, Ref. 29 profiled the 3D chromatin conformation of Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients and age-matched controls. However, due to the inherent flexibility of chromatin organization, identifying functionally relevant variations remains challenging, complicating the selection of changes to prioritize. To address this, we propose two complementary analyses to interrogate this dataset and gain insights into genome organization alterations associated with AD (data source 5). Primary Question: We will first utilize scCOE to derive embeddings of 3D chromatin organization at the single-cell level. These embeddings, optimized for predicting gene expression, are designed to capture critical structural features linked to regulatory mechanisms. To visualize these embeddings, we will apply UMAP dimensionality reduction for cells from both AD patients and controls. Observing significant differences in the structural organization between these groups may reveal disease-relevant changes in genome architecture. Downstream biophysical modeling may further elucidate the molecular determinants—potentially arising from epigenetic modifications or alterations in nucleosome positioning—that underlie the observed structural disruptions. Structural analysis of folding mechanisms involving zigzag, interdigitation, and hierarchical looping motifs, as well as modulation of nucleosome clutch patterns and nucleosome interactions can help determine the underlying biophysical rules that dictate genome folding and its relationship with gene expression. Secondary Question: Next, we will predict gene expression changes to directly compare differences between AD patients and controls. Elevated expression of specific genes in microglia has been implicated in AD pathology 30–32. By using scGEP to predict alterations in gene expression, we aim to determine whether such changes are attributable to modifications in 3D chromatin organization. This analysis complements the primary investigation, shifting the focus from global genome organization to the structural environment of individual genes. Together, these approaches may provide mechanistic insights into the causal relationships between chromatin architecture and gene expression, potentially identifying novel therapeutic strategies to restore normal expression levels. Outcomes. Technological advancement. Two innovative computational tools, scCOE and scGEP, will be produced. scCOE will greatly facilitate the analysis and interpretation of single-cell genome organization as this type of data becomes increasingly available in a variety of tissue samples. On the other hand, scGEP will allow the construction of single-cell multiomics data to better define cell types and characterize cellular diversity. Scientific advancement. The proposed research will transform our understanding of brain function, potentially identifying molecular markers for diseases such as Alzheimer’s. Our study will also provide insight into the connection between DNA sequence, 3D genome architecture, and gene expression. It will help address important questions regarding the significance of genome organization in regulating gene expression. Publications. Two manuscripts are expected, with one focusing on the technological innovation of leveraging multimodal models for understanding gene regulatory mechanisms and a second one focusing on the biological impact of genome organization in normal brain cell types and in malfunctioning cells from AD patients. Rationale for a working group approach. The proposed approach is inherently interdisciplinary, requiring expertise that extends beyond the capabilities typically found within a single group. Specifically, bioinformatics expertise (Noble Lab) is essential for organizing the genomics datasets from the three domains. Deep learning skills (Zhang Lab, Thirumalai Lab, and Schlick Lab) are crucial for constructing mechanistic models that integrate these data. Additionally, a thorough understanding of brain biology (Tan Lab) is necessary to interpret the findings derived from the AI models. The complexity of the project also requires a large cohort of researchers that is becoming increasingly challenging to support by any individual group. Rationale for NCEMS support. The NCEMS team will play a crucial role in collecting single-cell genomics data and integrating various assays into a unified, easily accessible database. Additionally, the computational resources provided by the center will facilitate the training of deep learning models. Requested resources. The model training will require 30,000 GPU hours, 9 million CPU hours, and 200 TB of data storage. We request the allocation of 33% of a NCEMS staff scientist's time per year. The scientist should possess expertise in single-cell genomics and deep learning. Proposed Timeline. Month Collect various single-cell genomic data across different human brain cell types. Process the 1-4 raw sequencing data into formats suitable for downstream analysis. Month Conduct tensor analysis for data imputation, pretrain the single-cell chromatin organization 5-12 embedding model (scCOE) using cell type-sorted single-cell datasets, and fine-tune the gene expression prediction model (scGEP) with co-assay data. Additionally, prepare a methodology manuscript detailing the development of these models. Month Investigate the variation in genome organization across brain cells and its correlation with 13-16 differences in gene expression. Additionally, analyze the variation in genome organization within a specific cell type and assess its influence on gene expression disparities. Month Investigate the differences in genome organization between individuals with Alzheimer's 17-24 disease and healthy controls, elucidating how structural variations influence gene expression. Prepare a manuscript detailing the functional importance of genome organization in cell differentiation and its role in disease progression.

proposals.proposal_title: MaiTool - LLM-powered bioinformatics tools for microbiome analysis
proposals.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT and BioGPT have revolutionized how researchers engage with scientific literature, offering capabilities such as extracting insights, summarizing methodologies, and identifying relevant publications. These models have applications in microbiome research, where they can assist in identifying datasets in repositories like MGnify and MG-RAST. However, LLMs lack the ability to directly analyze datasets, necessitating integration with bioinformatics tools to enable robust computational analysis. This project aims to develop MaiTool, a graphical interface that combines LLM capabilities with bioinformatics workflows for microbiome and ancient DNA research. MaiTool will enable users to explore publications, access public datasets via APIs, and perform dynamic analyses, integrating quality control measures to enhance reliability. Existing GPT systems (e.g., BioGPT, BioMedLM, and GeneGPT) will be evaluated and fine-tuned for microbiome applications. We will assess repositories such as HMP, IMG/M, and SRA for their suitability and develop APIs for seamless data access and integration. By addressing queries such as studies involving specific taxa, MaiTool will allow LLMs to retrieve literature while bioinformatics pipelines analyze and visualize dataset profiles. This approach aims to advance interdisciplinary research workflows and establish a new standard for AI-driven bioinformatics.
proposals.full_draft: Introduction and Goals The rise of large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT and BioGPT has revolutionized how 1,2 3 researchers engage with scientific publications. These models excel at understanding complex queries, enabling intelligent data retrieval tailored to project-specific needs. For instance, they can extract insights from publications, summarize methodologies, and, in the area of microbiome research, say, identify relevant datasets in repositories like MGnify and MG-RAST . However, 4,5 6 the direct analysis of datasets remains beyond the core capabilities of such systems. Integrating LLMs with traditional bioinformatics tools offers a promising solution, bridging the gap between natural language understanding and robust computational analysis. This integration could enable on-the-fly analyses of microbiome data while incorporating essential components like quality control to flag potential issues with datasets early in the pipeline. By combining LLMs’ contextual understanding with the computational power of bioinformatics tools, researchers could streamline workflows, ensuring efficient access to both published findings and actionable data. This project aims to develop a graphical interface “MaiTool” that facilitates the exploration of microbiome-related publications, provides seamless access to publicly available data, integrates quality control measures, and enables dynamic lightweight analyses. Such a system will empower researchers to make informed decisions efficiently, fostering innovation and collaboration in microbiome research and beyond (see Fig. 1). While the primary focus is on microbiome science, we also plan to explore extensions to computational challenges in analyzing ancient DNA sequences, including the microbiome analysis of ancient DNA samples. Figure 1. Integration between LLM and bioinformatics analysis tools via MaiTool. (a) Represents the LLM feature, and (b) illustrates the bioinformatics feature. Users can leverage both seamlessly through MaiTool for enhanced functionality and analysis. Proposed Activities: Data Collection, Curation, and Analysis Framework We propose to evaluate various GPT systems (BioGPT , BioMedLM and GeneGPT ) to determine 3 7 8 their effectiveness in assisting researchers with engaging and extracting insights from the scientific literature. Building on this foundation, we will identify 5–10 key use cases where the integration of bioinformatics tools—focused on quality assurance, data visualization, and lightweight computational analysis—can enhance the relevance and utility of the results. This approach aims to create a synergistic system that combines the contextual understanding of GPT models with the analytical power of bioinformatics to deliver targeted, actionable insights for microbiome research. In addition to evaluating existing GPT systems for their applicability in microbiome research, we will explore the feasibility of enhancing their performance through two approaches: either setting up our own large language model (LLM) tailored to specific microbiome research needs or fine-tuning existing (as mentioned in ref 1-3) open-source models. This exploration will help determine the optimal balance between leveraging pre-trained models and creating customized solutions to support advanced analysis and research workflows. In microbiome research, several public repositories provide access to microbiome data. Key repositories include MGnify , MG-RAST , the Human Microbiome Project (HMP) , the 4,5 6 9,12 Microbiome Atlas of Mothers and Infants (MAMI) , the Integrated Microbial Genomes and 13 Microbiomes system (IMG/M) and the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) from NCBI (further please 14 see Data Sources Table ), which is the most comprehensive resource for raw sequencing data. 15-16 We will evaluate each of these repositories to assess their suitability as sources of analysis results, focusing on their data accessibility, quality, and relevance to specific research needs. Additionally, we plan to develop software tools that leverage the APIs provided by these repositories to facilitate seamless access, integration, and utilization of their datasets within our system. This will enable efficient retrieval and analysis of microbiome data, supporting advanced research workflows. As an example, consider a user interested in determining whether there are studies that include a specific microbiome species of interest, such as the keystone gut species Christensenella minuta or oral species Methanobrevibacter oralis. Using the proposed system, a GPT model would first identify relevant publications that mention this species, extracting key information such as study descriptions, methodologies, and findings and data accessions from the literature. Simultaneously, using the reported accessions, a bioinformatics pipeline could access taxonomic profiles for the associated studies by accessing public microbiome datasets (along with metadata) through APIs. The pipeline may perform additional analyses, such as generating visualizations or conducting statistical analyses to explore patterns and relationships involving C. minuta. In addition, the GPT can provide a pipeline that the user can run themselves. Preliminary Data, Tools and Analytical Approaches We will conduct a systematic investigation of several GPT models, including BioGPT, BioMedLM, and GeneGPT, to evaluate their suitability for applications in microbiome analysis. For each model, we will assess its capabilities and explore the potential for fine-tuning to enhance support for data analysis tasks. Simultaneously, we will examine key microbiome data resources, including MG-RAST, HMP, IMG/M, MAMI, and datasets hosted at NCBI. This evaluation will focus on methods for extracting data, identifying analyses that can be performed dynamically, and establishing effective communication with the APIs provided by each resource. A third focus of our activities will be determining the best approach for implementing the interactive exploration tool MaiTool. MaiTool will serve as the primary interface for users, connecting seamlessly to an API for tasks such as LLM usage, data retrieval, and lightweight microbiome analysis. We intend to develop a standalone application using Java, JavaFX and Gluon, which would provide a highly responsive and feature-rich user experience, running on all platforms. The development of MaiTool will include a dedicated phase for comprehensive testing and usability studies to ensure the system meets the needs of researchers effectively. Outcomes This project will deliver several key outcomes: 1. Enhanced GPT for Microbiome and Ancient DNA Analysis: We will identify or fine-tune a GPT model specifically tailored to support research in microbiome and ancient DNA analysis. 2. Unified Microbiome Data API: A unified API will be developed to facilitate seamless access to microbiome data from multiple resources, streamlining data retrieval and integration. 3. Lightweight Bioinformatics Analysis Framework: We will create a bioinformatics framework to perform lightweight analyses on data obtained through the API, ensuring efficient and accessible computational workflows. (While a GPT may provide the description of a pipeline, the user will have to run it themselves, if they are interested in starting from scratch or raw data .) 4. Integrated AI-Bioinformatics System: A GPT system will be integrated with the developed tools to enable interactive access and analysis of microbiome data, bridging AI capabilities with bioinformatics functionality. 5. MaiTool Software for Analysis: We will develop a user-friendly software tool called MaiTool, designed to support both microbiome and ancient DNA analysis. MaiTool will provide an interactive interface for researchers, connecting seamlessly to APIs and integrating some analysis capabilities. 6. Insights into AI-Bioinformatics Integration: This project will provide valuable insights into the challenges and opportunities of integrating AI-driven systems with traditional bioinformatics software and algorithms, setting a foundation for future advancements in computational biology. These outcomes aim to advance microbiome research by enhancing data accessibility, analysis capabilities, and the synergy between AI and bioinformatics. Rationale for a working group approach This project focuses on integrating large language models (LLMs) with traditional data retrieval and bioinformatics analysis in the fields of microbiome and ancient DNA research. Achieving this goal requires expertise spanning multiple disciplines. • Daniel Huson specializes in developing algorithms and software for metagenomics and ancient DNA analysis, bringing essential computational and methodological expertise to the project. • Laura Weyrich contributes her extensive experience in the analysis of ancient DNA and ancient microbiomes, providing critical domain knowledge and practical insights into data interpretation and validation. • Maik Pietzner has a substantial track record in molecular epidemiology, spearheading the computational integration of multimodal ‘omics data sets in population-based studies with a particular focus on molecular quantitative trait loci. Together, this collaboration combines cutting-edge AI technology with expertise in microbiome and ancient DNA research, ensuring a robust and innovative approach to tackling these complex scientific challenges. Rationale for NCEMS support This project will require substantial computational resources to support the exploration of LLMs and microbiome resources. These resources will also be critical for hosting the GPT model used by MaiTool. Robust computational capacity is essential for running experiments, managing data workflows, and ensuring the scalability and responsiveness of the system. In addition, staff support will be vital for setting up computational workflows and implementing a REST API, ensuring seamless integration between components and efficient operation of the system. To foster innovation and collaboration, the project will also require support for short-term visitations between the labs of Working Group members. These visits will facilitate brainstorming, knowledge exchange, and the development of strategies to address the project’s interdisciplinary challenges. Requested resources The project requires 10–20 TB of storage for the enhancement and optimization of LLMs. Computational resources include 200–500 CPU cores and 10–30 GPUs, each with at least 100 GB of memory, to facilitate model development and optimization. RAM demands may increase up to 1–3 TB when models are combined. This will require approximately 200,000 CPU hours and 25000 GPU hours. We estimate that running the final model on a NCEMS host for users will require about 100GB of runtime memory, based on a estimated model size of 10 billion parameters. A staff scientist (up to 33% FTE) with expertise in LLMs will assist in model optimization, complementing the efforts of our existing experts. In addition, they can help ensure optimal utilization of NCEMS resources, including computational infrastructure, project management, and team science training. Proposed Timeline Year 1 Months 1–3: Conduct initial exploration of GPT models to assess suitability for microbiome and ancient DNA analysis. Begin initial exploration of microbiome resources (MG-RAST, HMP, IMG/M, MAMI, SRA) to evaluate data accessibility and API capabilities. Months 4–9: Design the framework for integrating LLMs with microbiome resources, including methods for extracting sample accessions and structuring data workflows. Months 6–12: Develop and implement APIs for seamless access to various microbiome resources, ensuring compatibility and efficient data retrieval. Months 10–12: Refine the accuracy of LLM-driven dataset selection. Improve presentation of analysis results, focusing on clarity and relevance for microbiome researchers. Year 2 Months 1–6: Develop and deploy a REST API to provide access to an LLM, supporting data access and bioinformatics analysis. Months 4–6: Build and implement the front-end interface for MaiTool, providing an alpha release for initial feedback. Months 7–9: Conduct comprehensive testing of the integrated system. Finalize documentation and address feedback to prepare for a beta release. Months 10–12: Publish results, describing the system’s design, capabilities, and applications. Release the fully functional system to the public.

proposals.proposal_title: Synthesizing gene expression data to create an atlas of bacterial cell states
proposals.abstract: Bacterial cells have evolved to adapt their molecular composition to maximize growth and survival. Our current knowledge of bacterial cell states is fragmented. Researchers often only analyze data they generate themselves—usually for just one strain under a limited number of conditions—because it is difficult to harmonize omics datasets collected with different technologies in different labs. Our NCEMS working group will synthesize bacterial gene expression data using machine learning to create a first-of-its-kind atlas of bacterial cell states. To manageably scale data collection and analysis, we will build from examining model Escherichia coli strains in lab conditions, to adding wild E. coli strains in natural environments such as the human gut, to including diverse bacterial species with additional cell states. We expect to identify distinct foci corresponding to bacterial growth states and lifestyles (e.g., replicating, starving, motile, biofilm, spore, viable but nonculturable) by mapping the organization and occupancy of cell state space with dimensional reduction approaches. We will examine to what extent the gene expression signatures of different cell states and the relationships among them are conserved during bacterial evolution. Finally, we will use this framework to create a classifier that predicts the cell state composition of a bacterial population from metatranscriptomic data. By following open-science practices, we will make our pipelines and datasets reusable and maintainable by the research community. Our project may reveal new bacterial cell states and ways that we can non-genetically reprogram bacteria to prevent them from adopting lifestyles that damage the environment and cause disease.
proposals.full_draft:
Introduction and Goals Bacterial cells modulate gene expression to adapt their physiology to changes in their environment, for example transitioning from actively replicating to quiescent states in response to nutrient exhaustion (e.g., exponential growth, stationary phase, sporulation) [1,2]. Much like cells within multicellular organisms, clonal bacterial populations can also diversify and differentiate into cell types with distinct phenotypes (e.g., biofilm/planktonic growth, motile/sessile forms, heterocysts/akinetes) [3,4]. However, it remains unclear to what extent bacterial cells have evolved to occupy a small number of discrete gene expression states that they abruptly transition between, or if they accommodate a more diffuse continuum of cell states and gradually shift their composition among them. Also, less is known about how different cell states and their gene expression profiles are related and conserved across species during evolution. Finally, it is possible that some bacterial cell states are unknown because our current knowledge is based on gene expression profiles from a limited selection of lab conditions and strains. The goals of our NCEMS working group are to test these hypotheses: 1. Bacterial cells occupy and cleanly transition between a small number of distinct states that are foci in the high-dimensional space defined by their molecular composition (e.g., gene expression vectors). 2. Fundamental principle components in bacterial cell state space (e.g., the growth-quiescence axis) have gene expression signatures that are conserved during evolution. 3. Bacterial cell states corresponding to specialized lifestyles found in only some species (e.g., biofilms, spores, heterocysts) evolved by subfunctionalization of these conserved cell states. 4. With a comprehensive bacterial cell state atlas organized by these principles, one can predict the proportions of cells occupying different states in complex populations (e.g., a gut microbiome). We will test and refine these hypotheses by using a synthesis approach at the mesoscale to create an atlas of bacterial cell states based on gene expression profiles. We will leverage existing datasets from both microarray [5,6] and RNA-seq [7,8] experiments—first for Escherichia coli lab strains, then more broadly for wild E. coli (including pathogens in host environments), and finally for ≥20 diverse species of bacteria—to examine the organization and occupancy of bacterial gene expression cell state space. Existing Datasets: Thousands of bacterial gene expression datasets have previously been collected in both E. coli-specific (OKgeneExpDB [9], E. coli Expression 2 [10], Ecomics [11], PRECISE [12,13]) and cross-species (COLUMBOS [14], iModulonDB [9]) compendia [15]. These databases include tens of thousands of gene expression profiles collected at multiple scales in terms of environmental variation (lab media compositions to animal host environments) and genetic variation (from single-gene mutants to lab-evolved strains with tens to thousands of mutations, to strains with different accessory gene content isolated from infections). Some databases have curated metadata and/or have reanalyzed raw data (microarray intensities or RNA-seq reads) in a consistent manner and discarded data that failed quality control. Unfortunately, most of these resources do not fully adhere to open-science principles [16]; their underlying code or information is not openly available/editable, or they are maintained by a single research group versus a multi-institutional community, and—as a result—few are still updated. Prior Analyses: Model-free machine learning (ML) approaches have been applied to these datasets to predict bacterial growth rates and infer growth conditions from gene expression profiles [11,17–19]. Another common goal is to infer co-regulated and co-transcribed ‘modules’ of genes to understand the organization of bacterial gene regulatory networks [20–23]. Some differences in gene expression in these datasets are planned (e.g., antibiotic treatments, genetic perturbations, different growth substrates). Other sources of technical variation (e.g., microarray version, sequencing technology, read length, RNA isolation method, ribosomal RNA depletion method) and unintended biological variation (contamination with other microbes, failure to remove genomic DNA, harvesting cells at a different growth phase) introduce systematic differences between datasets that may confound ML approaches. Robust data harmonization and quality control procedures are necessary to deal with these complications [11–14,24]. Project Significance: None of these prior studies have focused on identifying bacterial cell states, which we define as distinct growth or lifestyle states that cells adopt in a variety of environmental conditions. Operationally, we expect different cell states to have significant differences in the expression of ≥50 genes. For example, aerobic growth of E. coli planktonically as single cells in suspension would be one state—whether the carbon substrate is glycerol, glucose, or lactose—but this state is distinct from anaerobic growth, growth in a biofilm on a surface, starvation, etc. In the future, it may be possible to use single-cell RNA-seq to define these states, but such approaches currently have severe limitations for bacteria [7]. Instead, we posit that measuring gene expression for bacteria in defined culture conditions will often profile a nearly pure population of cells in one state or a mixture of cells in a limited number of states. Furthermore, some datasets will capture mutants that are ‘locked’ into or out of certain states (e.g., unable to form biofilms). Therefore, if we use dimensional reduction approaches to holistically understand the distribution of tens of thousands of samples in cell state space, we hypothesize that we can infer a comprehensive cell state atlas, even if the metadata is sparse or incomplete for many samples. Proposed Activities 1. Develop the open-source inGEST pipeline for harmonizing bacterial gene expression data sets Our synthesis project requires large numbers of high-quality gene expression datasets as input. We will process tens of thousands of RNA-seq and microarray datasets from raw data in the NCBI SRA and GEO databases in a uniform way, detect and exclude data that do not pass quality filtering criteria, and (ideally) correct for sources of technical variation. Fully featured pipelines for processing microarray data are implemented in a variety of R packages [25,26]. There are tutorials for reference-based RNA-seq processing pipelines for bacterial samples within the web-based Galaxy [27] and DOE Kbase [28] bioinformatics environments, and members of our team have built and used similar pipelines [29]. However, these packages/pipelines do not include the advanced quality control and harmonization steps needed when assembling databases with many thousands of samples from different research groups for comparison [11,20]. Furthermore, integration of microarray and RNA-seq data is rarely attempted. To meet this need, we will create the Integrative Gene Expression Synthesis Tool (InGEST). InGEST will perform the usual processing steps: background correction, scaling, and normalization for microarray data; read trimming, mapping, counting, and normalization for RNA-seq data. It will also have an advanced quality control (QC) dashboard that alerts a user to potential problems with specific samples (e.g., checking for DNA contamination by screening for abnormally high levels of antisense transcription, disagreement among biological replicates of one condition). Importantly, we will leverage the large amount of data we are analyzing to add functions to InGEST that identify and, if possible, correct for systematic technical biases (e.g., re-weighting gene expression based on read length [30,31]), which will be a novel and useful ML project in and of itself. With NCEMS guidance, we will design InGEST to be easily deployed (e.g., on CyVerse [32], using Docker containers, etc.) and maintained by the research community (by making code, documentation, and tutorials available on GitHub). 2. Apply dimensional reduction methods to create the Atlas of Bacterial Cell States To delineate cell states and how the space between them is populated, we will test unsupervised learning and dimensional reduction approaches that are commonly used with eukaryotic single-cell RNA-seq data to define cell populations in different tissues and developmental states [33,34]. These methods have been applied to understand the structure of bulk microbial gene expression datasets. For example Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) dimensional reduction has been used on microarray data from 1484 yeast single-gene knockout strains to discover genetic interactions [35]. First, we will focus solely on E. coli K-12 databases that have been curated by others (Datasets 1-4). We expect to first identify two main cell state ‘attractors’ for E. coli strains that correspond to aerobic exponential growth and stationary phase (Fig. 1A). By defining this growth-quescience axis, we can begin to organize additional components of variation to understand the candidate cell (sub)states, such as those that appear to be present in our preliminary analysis of 1055 RNA-seq datasets (Fig. 1B). As InGEST comes online, we will expand to non-lab E. coli strains and environments using data that has never been uniformly curated before (studies such as [37–41] in Datasets 5-6). We expect to identify cell states in this broader E. coli atlas that result from subfunctionalization of other main states (e.g., growth/starvation in biofilms has components of generic growth/quiescence states), which means we will also look for hierarchical structure in the main components of variation. One wrinkle is that different E. coli strains have different gene contents. We will use Orthofinder [42] to map orthologous genes across all E. coli strains so that we can maintain a consistent set of vector components for ML. Finally, we will examine ≥20 species for which there are ≥100 gene expression datasets each. These will include model organisms and human pathogens with additional cell states such as Pseudomonas and Vibrio spp. (biofilm and quorum sensing), Bacillus subtilis (sporulation and motility), Caulobacter crescentus (stalk/swarmer cells), and cyanobacteria (heterocysts). Again, we will create orthologous gene mappings using Orthofinder so that we can generate an expanded atlas and identify marker genes whose expression is associated with conserved/specialized states across species. This analysis has both transfer learning and novelty search components: we want to recognize states in a new bacterial species based on what we know from other species and also recognize when there are fundamentally new states that do not map onto our knowledge of state space built from other species. As we did for E. coli, we will pilot these analyses on databases curated by others (Datasets 7-8) as we InGEST our own datasets. 3. Create a classifier that predicts the distribution of cell states in a bacterial population Our atlas will define genes whose expression levels serve as cell state markers. Our final goal is to create classifiers (first for E. coli and then for any generic bacterial species) that predict the distribution of cell states in a gene expression dataset (e.g., this gut transcriptome has 80% biofilm and 20% planktonically dividing cells). For testing our methods we will first use synthetic data created by averaging together samples that are 100% in one state or another and then further test by comparing to the limited single-cell bacterial gene expression datasets that are available, e.g. for Staphylococcus aureus [43] and E. coli [44]. Lastly, we will apply our prediction framework to metatranscriptome data [45] from host-associated and environmental microbial communities (such as [46–48] in Datasets 5-6). Outcomes Significance to Field: By creating a unique Atlas of Bacterial Cell States, our project will reveal the fundamental ways that cell composition space is occupied and organized as bacteria respond to their environment and evolve. This project requires a multidisciplinary approach: to understand the structure of these extremely large datasets and to tease out biological meaning from technical red herrings. Our team has experts in systems biology, bioinformatics, bacterial genetics, evolution, mathematical modeling, theoretical and experimental biophysics, and machine learning. We also have deep expertise in bacterial physiology, including specifically for E. coli, Vibrio, Acinetobacter and other species. By analyzing much larger datasets than have ever been integrated before, we expect to find new biological organizing principles, and we may even discover novel cell states (e.g., phenotypes in cells exposed to antibiotics or other stressors). Our ultimate goal is to seed a collaborative effort to map and learn from a bacterial cell state atlas that spans the microbial tree of life, enabling a data-driven approach for classifying microbial cell states, lifestyles, and evolutionary transitions that continues into the future. Software and Data Products: In addition to these conceptual outcomes, we envision three, related software/data products, one corresponding to each of our primary activities. 1. Integrative Gene Expression Synthesis Tool (InGEST). This tool will make it possible for researchers to perform quality control and correct for technical/biological complications that can confound analyzing large sets of gene expression data generated by different labs/researchers. 2. Atlas of Bacterial Cell States. This dataset will synthesize our knowledge of how bacterial cells differentiate and modulate their molecular composition in response to the environment. The first release will focus on E. coli. The second will expand to other bacterial species. It will include tools for interactively visualizing relationships between cell states and relevant marker genes. 3. Bacterial Cell Population Classifier. This tool will package the relationships inferred in the atlas into a tool that can take any bacterial gene expression dataset and predict its cell state composition, including RNA-seq or microarray data collected for communities containing multiple species. For all three products, we will leverage NCEMS support to apply open-science principles so that other researchers can update and expand them into the future. Code and datasets will be open-source, licensed for reusability, well-documented, and freely available in versioned releases with citable DOIs. We will have instructions for integrating and contributing new code and datasets. We will advertise these resources through our publications and professional networks to engage our communities with the aim of building a sufficiently engaged user base that there will be an impetus to continue to update them. Future Work: Our analysis framework can be readily extended to other microbes, such as fungi and archaea, and to examine other types of omics cell composition information, for example proteomics or metabolomics datasets. Future work could test extending the datasets and analyses to those layers and integrating multiomics information when it is available. Knowledge of microbial cell states and how they are related could guide new approaches that seek to non-genetically reprogram bacterial behaviors—perturbing them to change cell states from harmful to benign ones, for example. Rationale for NCEMS support Our project will synthesize existing data at the mesoscale: it will use machine learning approaches to understand and visualize gene expression states of bacterial cells. This endeavor requires creating scalable and reproducible pipelines for ingesting, harmonizing, validating, and analyzing gene expression datasets. We want to create sustainable, open-science resources on a scale that none of our research groups could achieve on our own. Prior attempts at integrating even just E. coli gene expression data have all proven to be short-lived. We need NCEMS support to implement best practices so that this bioinformatics infrastructure and these datasets are reusable and maintainable by the community. Additionally, while we have ML expertise on our team, we think that breakthroughs in analyzing these datasets will require new approaches that may not (yet) be familiar to us, particularly for visualizing and quantitatively analyzing the data to define cell state foci and their relationships to one another. Requested resources We expect to primarily need computational resources for downloading and processing RNA-seq datasets. A typical RNA-seq dataset is 0.2-2 Gb of Illumina reads in FASTQ format. Not all datasets need to be persistently stored. They can be downloaded from the NCBI Sequence Read Archive and processed in batches. We estimate that it will take at most 30 minutes of CPU time for our pipeline to download and process a typical dataset (<300,000 CPU hours total). Microarray gene expression measurements consist of intensity measurements with a negligible disk footprint and processing needs. Similarly, machine learning for our project (e.g., dimensional reduction by UMAP and other methods) can be completed for tens of thousands of samples on a laptop, though it is possible more advanced approaches will need additional computational resources. The final data resource we envision consists of metadata for each sample, a matrix of read counts or hybridization signals for each gene in each sample, and a set of annotated reference genomes and gene orthologs. It will be small enough (estimated <200 Mb) to store in a GitHub repository and archive in Zenodo. Proposed Timeline We request 2 years of support. The first year will focus on E. coli. The second year will expand to other bacteria. We will develop our pipeline for harmonizing datasets in parallel with testing machine learning approaches for analyzing the organization and occupancy of cell states using existing datasets. Months Milestones 1-6 ● Use ML methods to examine technical and biological variation in existing datasets. ● Create inGEST for quality-checking and harmonizing bacterial gene expression datasets. ● inGEST ≥10,000 gene expression datasets for the E. coli cell state atlas. 7-12 ● Use ML methods for reducing dimensionality to identify E. coli cell states and the fundamentand the sets of marker genes that define these states and their relationships. ● Submit initial publication describing the inGEST pipeline and the E. coli cell state atlas. 13-21 ● inGEST ≥10,000 additional gene expression datasets from ≥20 other bacterial species. ● Use ML to identify new cell states and relationships between conserved cell states and whether the same marker genes define these states across multiple species. 22-24 ● Develop the cell state classifier and apply it to gene expression data from bacterial species not included in the training set and to metatranscriptomic gene expression data. ● Submit a second publication describing the multispecies atlas of bacterial cell states and our analysis of the conservation of states and origins of new specialized states.
