proposals.proposal_title: Energetic Origins of Connectivity within Protein Interaction Networks
proposals.abstract: At least 10% of cellular proteins are intrinsically unstable and fold with marginal efficiency. In the cell, these proteins are preferentially engaged by chaperones and quality control proteins that refold or degrade them. Similarly, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) preferentially interact with specific partners that they require for folding and function. Such proteins must exhibit bias in the types of protein-protein interactions they form within the cell. We therefore hypothesize that the emergent scaling properties of protein interaction networks arise, in part, from the promiscuous interactions formed by unstable proteins and the obligate interactions formed by IDPs. To test this hypothesis, we will analyze existing large-scale interactome datasets to explore the context of unstable and disordered proteins within interaction networks. By extending this approach to evaluate how proteins with various conformational properties are distributed across several unicellular and multicellular networks, we aim to uncover generalizable insights into how protein biophysics shapes network architecture. Additionally, by mapping the centrality of proteins involved in various supramolecular organization regimes, we will identify topological niches associated with the occurrence of liquid-liquid phase separation and quinary structure. Finally, to determine the extent to which these biases constrain network evolution, we will utilize genetic algorithms to explore how changes in the stability of the proteome restrict the topologies that are accessible through evolution. Together, these investigations will provide insights into the role of protein stability and binding efficiency in the evolution of PPI networks and how this relates to the molecular mechanisms of evolution.
proposals.full_draft: A. Introduction and Goals. Over the past 20 years, emergent evidence has suggested the architecture, scaling, and topologies of protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks are similar across prokaryotes and eukaryotes alike.1 For instance, one apparent property of PPI networks is a scale-free topology in which the interactions (i.e. edges) among proteins (i.e. nodes) follow a power law distribution.1–4 While the true scaling of PPI networks may be obscured by experimental biases,5 it seems clear that a sizable proportion of proteins form a small number of discrete interactions (i.e. low degree)- there are relatively few “hubs” that form numerous promiscuous interactions. It has been suggested that selection pressures have refined resilient network topologies in which cooperative metabolic pivots can be achieved through the regulation of handful of nodes that connect clusters.6–9 To ensure robustness, the few high-degree hubs that do exist within these networks often have functionally redundant paralogs in order to minimize the fitness effects of deleterious mutations within hub proteins. In biological systems, “party hubs” are larger proteins that form continuous interactions within functional complexes and exhibit co-expression, while “date hubs” are smaller proteins that form transient interactions with different partners, serving as bridges between network modules and showing low co-expression. Importantly, several studies suggest that the presence of IDRs is a common feature of eukaryotic hub proteins. IDPs in both party and date hubs can introduce new specificities, which may help differentiate between single- and multiple-interface hubs. The position of a node within a network is also critical to its overall function.4,10 This feature can be described by its betweenness centrality- a measure for how often a node lies on the shortest paths between pairs of other nodes. Nodes with high betweenness centrality act as bottlenecks and do not necessarily exhibit high degree. Overall, betweenness centrality and other related node descriptors can be broadly categorized into three types: neighborhood-based, path-based, and iterative refinement-based centralities. The magnitudes of these connections ultimately depends on the number of complexes they form, which is physically dictated by their biophysical properties and cellular abundance. We therefore believe the integration of multiscale biophysical to cellular network descriptors will reveal how the intrinsic properties of proteins give rise to the topological properties of PPI networks and their biological function. Notably, there are currently a wide variety of publicly available interactome data that can be used to construct and analyze PPI networks (see Datasets Table). Despite variations in the completeness of such data, networks constructed using current interactome data for both single cell organisms (e.g. S. cerevisiae) and a variety of higher organisms ranging from A. thaliana to H. sapiens have already provided detailed insights into how pathogens coopt hubs and bottlenecks.11–14 It remains unclear how cells achieve and maintain preferred architectures given that the nodes within them continue to adaptively evolve new structural interactions. While the evolutionary dynamics of PPI networks remain poorly understood, we understand a great deal about the evolutionary constraints on protein structure and function. For instance, it is known that most mutations destabilize native protein structure in a manner that ultimately reduces protein stability.15,16 Thus, individual protein structures can typically only accommodate certain sequences of stabilizing and destabilizing mutations- sequential destabilizing mutations are generally lost to purifying selection.17–22 Based on these considerations, we propose to develop a physical framework that describes how the properties of PPI networks emerge from the physical properties of the proteins within them. For example, increases in abundance could potentially compensate for low stability and weak binding efficiency, while changes that weaken binding may promote promiscuous interactions. Protein variants that visit low-stability regimes may also be prone to forming new chaperone interactions,23,24 which could potentially facilitate their transition between clusters. In the context of a PPI network, one could also imagine that purifying selection may be weaker for low-degree proteins and/ or high-degree proteins that are functionally redundant. We suspect that networks must contain niches that can accommodate variations in protein stability in a manner that may preserve topology. Models of PPI networks that account for such factors may therefore provide insight into how evolutionary modifications of protein stability, binding efficiency and cellular abundance contribute to network robustness. How can modular protein clusters that execute a common biochemical pathway maintain their connectivity in the face of genetic drift? Do chaperone hubs act as anchors for network topology? Are unstable clients that engage multiple chaperones more likely to transition from one cluster to another? In contrast, do IDPs that rely on specific interactors become anchored to a specific cluster? In this work, we outline a series of investigations that will repurpose interactome data to build network models for diverse organisms, then evaluate the topological context of proteins with divergent biophysical properties. Our investigations will provide new insights into the biophysical mechanisms that give rise to the emergent properties of biological networks. Goal 1. Determine how protein stability biases interaction networks. Across evolutionary timescales, most proteins will inevitably traverse low-stability regimes in which they may become predisposed to chaperone interactions.17 A reliance on shared chaperone hubs can generate indirect proteostatic couplings that may alter protein solubility and function.25 However, it remains unclear how client-chaperone interactions shape network topology or whether the proteostatic fates of unstable proteins may hinge upon their network localization. We hypothesize that unstable proteins exhibit enhanced connectivity within PPI networks as a result of their interactions with the proteostasis network. To test this hypothesis, we will leverage high quality interactome data3 to construct a high-resolution map of the S. cerevisiae PPI network then utilize computational protein stability estimates26–28 to evaluate the connectivity of unstable proteins. To validate our analyses, the results will be cross referenced against limited proteolysis mass spectrometry (LiP-MS),29 proteomic half-life measurements,30 and abundance31 measurements. Finally, using annotations for sub-cellular localization, we will repeat these exercises using organelle-specific networks to see whether these trends diverge within cellular compartments. Goal 2. Survey the interactions formed by unstable proteins and IDPs within divergent PPI networks. Higher organisms have evolved elaborate cellular proteostasis networks that help support the folding of more structurally diverse proteomes. These adaptations effectively increase the “buffering capacity” of the proteome.32 However, it is unclear whether changes in the composition of the proteostasis network could potentially alter the interactions formed by unstable proteins and/ or IDPs. It is also unclear whether such proteins remain beholden to specific chaperones over extended biological time scales. We hypothesize that unstable proteins will form promiscuous chaperone interactions and will form more interactions overall relative to IDPs in all networks. To test this hypothesis, we will first extend the approaches detailed in Goal 1 to map the PPI networks of various organisms, then characterize the topological context of the unstable proteins and IDPs within each proteome. We will then compare the chaperones that associate with homologous client proteins across divergent interactomes. By comparing these metrics among stable, unstable, and disordered proteins, we will determine whether unstable proteins and their evolutionary ancestors exhibit “preferential attachment” to chaperone hubs1 in a manner that maintains their positions and/ or preserves the scaling of the network. Goal 3. Determine how marginally stable and unstable proteins constrain PPI network topology. The biophysical properties of many client-chaperone interactions diverge from those of the typical sorts of PPIs that give rise to biochemical function. Many proteins with elaborate assembly pathways ultimately develop a functional dependence on specific chaperones.33 We hypothesize that these persistent chaperone interactions can restrain the topology of the interactome. We will test this hypothesis by using genetic algorithms to generate evolutionary trajectories of various networks that are designed to recapitulate the interplay between protein stability, binding efficiency, and protein abundance yet feature tunable constraints on the number of chaperone hubs and the persistence of chaperone-client interactions. We will then evaluate whether any degeneracy among client-chaperone interactions emerges across simulated time scales that resemble those observed in natural PPI networks. The results will reveal whether the quality control interactions of unstable proteins ultimately constrain PPI networks. B. Proposed Activities. Our approach to achieving these goals will proceed as follows: Generation of PPI Network Models. (Mukhtar). The Mukhtar group has already curated comprehensive interaction data and used it to construct network models for A. thaliana and H. sapiens using a custom software pipeline.6,7 We will use this approach to build network models for E. coli, S. cerevisiae, and C. elegans using select in vivo interactome data or ex vivo co-fractionation/ high-throughput IP-MS interactome data.3 To identify the most critical nodes, we will then use these models to calculate eight distinct centrality measures that span the three categories (described above) for each protein including degree centrality, betweenness centrality, eigenvector centrality, closeness centrality, load centrality, PageRank, and weighted k-shell decomposition. Each of these metrics capture a unique aspect of node importance. While most calculations will use Python, the weighted k-shell decomposition will rely on Cytoscape. We will also use node prioritization algorithms that identify influential based on their relationships with other nodes. For these purposes, we will use the Mukhtar labs CentralityCosDist algorithm, which ranks nodes based on a combination of centrality measures and seed nodes. We will also use MCODE to extract clusters in conjunction with the network visualization tools in Cytoscape. We will also integrate single-cell and stimuli-responsive data within GEO-NCBI to construct and parameterize context-dependent interactomes with the use of contextual AI models for single-cell protein biology.34 Finally, we will carry out functional enrichment analyses using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA), WikiPathways, Gene Ontology (GO) biological processes, and ClueGO. These approaches leverage robust computational tools, advanced centrality measures, and biological data to generate rich maps of PPI networks detailing the context of unstable proteins. Generation of Biophysical Descriptors of the Proteome. (Schlebach). To determine whether proteins with certain structural properties tend to cluster within PPI networks, we will compare each protein’s network centrality features to a variety protein stability and disorder predictions. We will first utilize the DisProt database along with the critical assessment of intrinsic disorder (CAID) prediction portal35 in order to distinguish proteins that adopt a unique fold from those that persist as IDPs. For proteins that are predicted to fold, we will then utilize two distinct approaches to estimate absolute protein stability. We will first leverage recent advances in generative modeling28 to generate structural predictions for absolute stability based on a comprehensive, proteome-wide set of AlphaFold2 models.36 While this state-of-the-art approach generates useful stability predictions from structural models (1.5 kcal/ mol mean error), its performance is only accurate for single domain proteins of less than 150 AA.28 For larger proteins we will instead rely on simplified length-based approximations for protein stability.26,27 To spot check questionable predictions, we will utilize DBFOLD,37 which generates simulation-based stability approximations, to accept or reject outliers. We will then utilize these coarse stability descriptors to parse proteins into classes based on whether they are stable, unstable, or intrinsically disordered. Pairwise Fishers exact tests will then be used to determine whether high centrality proteins are enriched within any of these classes. Finally, to ensure the robustness of any potential enrichments, we will vary the threshold values used to classify the proteins then repeat the analysis. Our results will reveal whether unstable and/ or disordered proteins form biased interactions within the network. Moreover, this approach can be generalized by incorporating a variety of additional node classifications (i.e. chaperones, LLPS proteins, etc.) to determine whether certain biochemical phenomena are associated with high centrality. Finally, we will incorporate LiP-MS,29 cellular turnover,30 and expression31 data into these analyses to assess whether centrality features are associated with deviations in proteostasis. Generation of evolutionary models of PPI networks. (Serohijos) The Serohijos and Shaknovich labs have developed integrative models of protein evolution that accounts for biophysics, cellular properties, and population genetics.38–49 These will be scaled to the entire proteome and to account for chaperones and IDR contributions. These models have three components- a fitness function, a quantitative description of effects of random mutations, and evolutionary algorithm implementing selection. The fitness function will reflect the cellular intuition of the functionality of natively folded protein and thus depends on P_native=1/(1+e^(βγΔG_f)), where ΔG_f is folding free energy and γ reflects the chaperone’s role in promoting folding.41,42,45,49–51 The number of functional copies of protein complexes (edge) in the network is F_ij=D_ij(P_int,ij)(P_native,i)(P_native,j),38–40 where the last two factors are the folding stability of proteins i and j. P_int,ij is the Boltzmann probability that the proteins are docked in their functional configuration and reflects the contribution of chaperones in promoting PPIs. D_ij is effective concentration of the complex formed by i and j and is a function of cellular abundances and binding efficiency (data from Goals 1 & 2). Since a protein engages in multiple interactions, the fitness function is solved iteratively over the entire proteome to satisfy law of mass action.38–40 Next, the evolutionary algorithm generates random mutations,51 whose effects on folding stability and binding affinity will be quantified using a combination of prior literature15,52–55 and biophysical descriptors above. Effects of mutations on abundance will be informed by extensive expression data of genomic variants.56 Then, we calculate the selective advantage of the random mutation based on the fitness of wildtype and mutant, s=(f_wt−f_mutant)/f_wt and the likelihood of fixation based on Kimura formula57 that captures positive and purifying selection in evolutionary algorithms. C. Outcomes. Several emergent properties of PPI networks appear to be conserved across all kingdoms of life.1 While the scaling architectures may offer biological utility, it remains unclear how the thousands of biophysically diverse proteins within these networks manage to achieve this sort of connectivity. The proposed investigations will provide basic insights into the manner in which variations in the biophysical properties of proteins shapes interaction networks and contributes to their emergent properties. We anticipate our results will reveal that unstable proteins will exhibit higher degree relative to stable proteins and that these proteins will cluster around a relatively small number of chaperone hubs. As this biophysical limitation can often be overcome with a single stabilizing mutation, we anticipate that unstable proteins will exhibit higher mobility across biologically diverse PPI networks. In contrast, we expect that intrinsically disordered proteins that rely on specific interaction partners will retain their relative positions across biologically diverse PPI networks. We also anticipate that these biophysical properties will be strongly affected by cellular properties, such as the abundance and localization of the binding partners. Finally, we expect that our simulations will reveal that the biased interactions formed by these two classes of proteins will impose dominant constraints on network topology. Together, these investigations will establish a new emerging frontier in systems biophysics. D. Working Group Rationale. The proposed investigations are truly interdisciplinary and will merge computational biophysics with systems biology. Together, the strengths of the Schlebach lab in protein biophysics and structural informatics along with the expertise of the Mukhtar lab in the graphical analysis of PPI networks will provide the complementary expertise to carry out Goals 1 and 2. Goal 3 will leverage the expertise of the Serohijos lab in evolutionary biophysics to gain insights into how these factors impact changes in these networks over time. Finally, the Shakhnovich lab will provide complementary expertise and domain knowledge that will help connect these concepts to organizational paradigms in metabolism. Bringing our groups together will also increase the number of trainees that potentially stand to benefit from this collaboration. Rationale for NCEMS Support. As the proposed investigations represent a fundamentally new direction for our groups, we currently lack the dedicated resources to advance this project. NCEMS staff support will facilitate the curation, integration, and analysis of these data. The requested computational resources will help us run the analyses described herein. Administrative support will ensure our collaboration reaches its full productive potential. Requested Resources. We request the following project-specific support over two years: -Staff Scientist Support- one 33% FTE per year -Staff Scientist Assistant Support- one 50% FTE per year, preferably with domain knowledge in biochemistry and structural biology -Cyberinfrastructure Resources- 10 TB storage, 1,000,000 CPU hours -Travel Budget- $5k per year to support for one in-person meeting per year -Publication Cost Support- $5k total to cover article publishing charges -Personnel Exchange: $5k/ year to support the exchange of trainees between member labs Proposed Timeline. Key milestones over the two years of work includes: 1. PPI network construction for E. coli, S. cerevisiae, A. thaliana, C. elegans, and H. sapiens 2. Calculation of centrality measures for each node within each network 3. Generation of biophysical estimates for protein stability across each proteome 4. Annotation of chaperones, oligomers, and IDPs within each network 5. Statistical enrichment calculations for centrality measures in unstable proteins and IDPs 6. Development of genetic algorithms to simulate the evolutionary trajectories of networks

proposals.proposal_title: Elucidating emergent structures in cellular RNA-protein interaction networks
proposals.abstract: Messenger RNA molecules are constantly bound by proteins that regulate all aspects of their function, including their processing, localization, translation, and degradation1. These mRNA-protein complexes (mRNPs) can also interact with each other and assemble into higher-order structures that play critical roles in cellular organization and response to environmental stimuli1-3. Despite their importance, we lack a comprehensive map of these cellular RNA-protein interaction networks at both the nano and micro scales. Years of efforts by researchers across the globe have yielded a large, but disjointed, collection of datasets that map different aspects of RNA-protein interactions. Currently, we lack tools to integrate these datasets, preventing their synthesis into a coherent and interpretable interaction map. Here, we propose to develop tools to combine disparate data types to build transcriptome-wide maps of mRNPs, and their higher-order interactions within cells. We will then apply these tools to gain insights into long-standing biological mysteries, including the impacts of synonymous mutations and cell-type specific effects of widely expressed RNAs.
proposals.full_draft:
Introduction and Goals: RNA is Life’s prime messenger molecule of genetic information. While for all organisms—minus some viral exceptions—DNA provides long-term storage, RNA is its direct output, relaying this genetic info into molecular actions 4, 5 . Messenger RNA (mRNA) instructs the ribosomes to fabricate the plethora of proteins that carry out most cellular and biochemical functions. There are also socalled non-coding RNAs (ncRNA) that serve mostly structural, enzymatic or regulatory functions 6 . For example, long non-coding RNAs (lncRNA) like NEAT1 RNA recruit specific sticky proteins to form biochemically distinct subcellular compartments called paraspeckles—a type of biomolecular condensate 7 . Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) is a prime example of a catalytic RNA or ribozyme, and small RNAs like micro RNAs (miRNA) can regulate the abundance of other RNA species 8 . While it is clear that RNAs carry out essential functions in cells, they do not act alone 9 . It is well understood that RNAs are never “naked” in the cellular environment 1, 9 . Cells harbor hundreds of RNA-binding proteins that can decorate RNA molecules depending on their specific nucleotide sequence and secondary structure or simply based on the inherent negative charge of the RNA backbone 2, 9 . So, for every RNA molecule, from the moment it emerges from the polymerase transcription bubble, there will be a complex, spatially and temporally dynamic set of protein interaction partners that dictate its processing and structural remodeling, its transport through the cell, its biochemical function and eventual decay. Given that most of these RNA-protein complexes (RNPs) are considered to form their own single entity, they each present as a wildly complex and dynamic microcosm of different proteins interacting with a single RNA 10, 11 . Moreover, all of these proteins can have specific or non-specific interactions with each other—based on their biochemical composition, structure and unstructure or disorder—that affect each other’s behavior and the eventual mRNP composition 1 . Needless to say, given such complexity and the breadth of potential RNA-RNA, RNA-protein and protein-protein interactions it is highly unlikely that the sum of each of these individual components is sufficient to explain the outcome. On the contrary, new unexpected behaviors are bound to emerge from this complexity. We argue that mRNPs are one of the best examples to study emergent behavior in an essential cellular process for life on this planet. The goal of this project is to create a roadmap to understand the composition of the cell’s many thousands of RNPs, focusing specifically on mRNA-protein complexes (mRNPs), and their higher order interactions, by integrating available experimental RNA-RNA, RNA-protein and protein-protein interaction data using recent state-of-the-art computational tools for predicting protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions (Figure 1). We postulate that this will allow us to come up with a predictive framework to understand the emergent behaviors that arise from mRNP composition. We will validate the predictive power of our framework through the lens of (1) human sequence variation dictating RNA abundance and splicing, (2) the robustness or sensitivity of splicing to RNA-binding protein loss, and (3) the composition of higher-order biomolecular structures that form when individual mRNPs form environmentally-triggered condensates. Proposed Activities Aim 1: Integrate publicly available datasets to build a transcriptome-wide map of mRNPs. In cells, mRNA molecules are constantly bound by proteins, which regulate nearly every aspect of their processing, localization, translation, and degradation1, 2. As such, there have been numerous efforts to systematically map mRNA-protein interactions in cells, resulting in a long list of large-scale and transcriptome-wide datasets12-18. These datasets have been generated through many different experimental techniques, each measuring a different aspect of these interactions, making it nontrivial to compare and combine them. Without the ability to integrate these measurements, we lack a transcriptome-wide “mRNP map” — i.e., we have a fragmented and incomplete understanding of the composition and architecture of mRNPs, despite an abundance of data. We hypothesize that a transcriptome-wide mRNP map would help mechanistically explain several long-standing biological mysteries, including how synonymous mutations and mutations in non-coding regions of RNA molecules impact cellular function, and why mutations in RNA molecules that are widely expressed have highly cell-type specific effects. Here, to address this challenge, we will (1) develop a method to integrate disparate datasets, which report on multiple aspects of RNA-protein interactions, to build complete mRNP maps; (2) apply this method to build a transcriptome-wide mRNP map for K562 cells; and (3) use this map to predict and develop mechanistic hypotheses for RNA fate upon genetic perturbation. 1.1. Develop a method to integrate disparate datasets to build complete mRNP maps: Our goal is to develop a computational method that takes a set of disparate RNA-protein interaction datasets as input and outputs an mRNP map (list of mRNA molecules, bound proteins, including specific nucleotides at which they are bound). We will first collect all publicly available datasets that report on different aspects of RNA-protein interactions in cells12-18, detailed in our Datasets Table (Source ID 1-7). To integrate the datasets, we will develop a set of linked features that connect each pair of data modalities. A linked feature is a shared characteristic or metric that is either directly measured by both datasets or can be reliably inferred from their respective measurements. These linked features will then serve as “anchors” for data normalization and integration. We will test multiple different linked features and normalization approaches and assess their accuracy using the β-actin mRNP, which has been extensively characterized at relatively high-resolution19. By linking all data modalities to transcriptome-wide mapping of proteinbinding sites (e.g., POP-seq)16, this will result in a transcriptome-wide mRNP map. 1.2. Build a transcriptome-wide mRNP map for K562 cells: We will extend the tool developed in 1.1 to identify additional proteins that may be a part of each mRNP. We will identify protein interaction partners for each protein member of each mRNP by utilizing data from existing protein-protein interaction databases (e.g., BioGRID20, Datasets Table Source ID 12), and by predicting protein-protein interactions with AlphaFold for structured domains21, and with FINCHES for interactions between intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)22. Input to this tool will be a list of mRNP components and a parameter “N”, specifying the number of layers of connections to predict. For example, N=1 would predict all direct interactions of the mRNP components; N=2 would predict direct interactions as well as the interacting partners of those components. We will apply this tool, with N=1, with the data described in 1.1 that was collected for K562 cells to build a complete mRNP map for this cell type. We will also assess the signalto-noise for each dataset by comparing to corresponding high-resolution measurements for the extensively characterized β-actin mRNP19, so we can assign confidence scores to each interaction within the mRNP map. 1.3. Predicting RNA fate upon genetic perturbation: To test the predictive power of our framework regarding the regulation of RNAs upon perturbation of the system, we will follow two approaches. First, there is a wealth of human genetic variation that is linked to the abundance or splicing of an mRNA, expression and splicing quantitative trait loci, eQTL and sQTL, respectively23-25. Can our framework, which takes into account the different proteins and regulatory RNAs that bind a transcript, explain the effect of a point mutation in the sequence on its eventual abundance or splicing? For example, a mutation may affect an RNA-binding protein or miRNA binding site. Second, we will ask whether our framework reproduces effects seen in RNA-binding protein knockout data12. Can this data inform the predictions we made for eQTLs and sQTLs? Addressing these questions will indicate the predictive power of our framework and highlight areas where more data may need to be collected. After addressing these validation questions, we will use our model to make mechanistic predictions as to why mutations in RNA molecules that are widely expressed have highly cell-type specific effects26. Aim 2: Map out interaction networks of mRNPs. This aim seeks to identify the network of interactions between mRNPs, by addressing the following questions: (1) What is the mesoscale interaction network that a given mRNP belongs to? (2) Can we predict what subcellular compartments, such as biomolecular condensates, that a given mRNP would localize to? (3) Can we predict the compositional variability of condensates such as stress granules based on mRNP networks? To this end, our team will pioneer new approaches to map out higher-order interaction networks of mRNPs within cells. We hypothesize that the physicochemical characteristics of mRNPs encode their spatiotemporal properties within living cells. 2.1. Deploy our mRNP map tool to identify emergent structures of mRNPs: Our goal is to predict higher-order interaction networks of mRNPs. Using the mRNP map tool generated in Aim 1.2, we will determine the network of proteins associated with each mRNP (i.e., N>1). Protein interaction networks will be analyzed using clustering or community detection algorithms to group proteins into mesoscale networks based on shared physical properties, such as interaction motifs or binding affinities. Our identified clusters will be validated using mass spectrometry crosslinking data and proximity labeling datasets (Datasets Table, Source ID 7, 10, 11)18, 27, 28. Finally, we will compare the identified clusters to known protein compositions of individual condensates to assess their alignment with specific biomolecular compartments. Ultimately, we anticipate that this approach will aid in identifying new condensates. 2.2. Predict mRNP partitioning into biomolecular condensates: Leveraging databases such as CD- Code and RNA Granule Database (Datasets Table, Source ID 13, 14)29-31, we will curate a subset of proteins and RNAs known to localize to stress granules and P bodies, gathering their physicochemical properties, including sequence composition, charge distribution, hydrophobicity, structural disorder, RNA-binding domains, and low-complexity domains. In parallel, we will use the tool developed in Aim 1.1 to identify mRNPs associated with both types of condensates. Based on the curated data, we will design model condensates that incorporate averaged physiological features representative of stress granules and P bodies. Using the Mpipi model, we will perform residue-resolution molecular dynamics simulations to measure the partitioning coefficients of approximately 2,500 mRNPs across both model condensates32. This data will then be used to train a neural network capable of predicting the partition coefficient of any given mRNP into either stress granules or P bodies. The model will be validated against existing transcriptome datasets, such as RNA-seq and RIP-seq data, that profile RNAs enriched in stress granules and P bodies under specific conditions (detailed in our Datasets Table, Source ID 8-9)31. 2.3 Predicting stress granule composition across cell types: Stress granules are some of the most widely studied biomolecular condensates with many datasets on their protein and RNA composition being readily available31, 33. While most of these studies have been performed in U2OS cells, datasets on other cell lines and primary or iPSC-derived cells exist (Datasets Table, Source ID 9, 13, 14)29-31, 33. Based on the RNA and protein abundance of specific cells, can we use our framework to predict the variance and similarity in stress granule composition? Addressing this question will help us uncover the molecular rules that dictate condensate formation and composition in both a cell-specific and non-specific manner. Outcomes Our work will result in open-source tools for integrating disparate data sources to map RNA-protein interactions at the nano-scale (Aim 1) and the meso-scale (Aim 2), as well as specific applications of these tools to explain emergent structures and functional data. The specific outcomes from each sub-aim are detailed below: Aim 1.1: An open-source tool for predicting transcriptome-wide mRNP maps from disparate datasets reporting on different aspects of RNA-protein interactions. As more data continues to be collected for new cell types and in different conditions, this method can easily be applied to build new transcriptome-wide mRNP maps. Aim 1.2: A transcriptome-wide mRNP map/database for K562 cells. For each mRNA molecule expressed in K562 cells, the map will contain a list of all proteins that are bound, including the specific nucleotides that they are bound to, approximate binding affinities of the RNA-protein interactions, the domains or specific residues of the bound protein that actually interact with the RNA molecule, a list of proteins that interact with RNA-bound proteins, and a confidence score for each interaction. Aim 1.3: Assessment of the predictive power of our mRNP map to explain the functional consequences of genetic perturbations. We will use any “failures” of our models to highlight gaps in our current knowledge and to propose new experiments which may be helpful for directing future work within the broader RNP research community. Aim 2.1: A database of microscale clusters composed of mRNPs and their interaction partners, providing context-specific details for each mRNP in our mRNP database. This resource will enable the research community to predict how mRNPs contribute to the formation of functional mesoscale structures. Aim 2.2: An open-source tool to predict the relative localization of any mRNP to stress granules and P bodies. This tool will empower the research community to uncover how physicochemical properties of mRNPs influence their localization to these essential subcellular compartments, providing critical insights into the functional landscape of biomolecular condensates. Aim 2.3: A model that predicts cell type specific stress granule composition. This work in this aim will also provide a roadmap for modeling cell type specific composition of other condensates. Rationale for working group approach: This project requires several distinct areas of expertise that go far beyond the skill sets that any individual lab would have. In addition to general subject-matter expertise in RNA-protein interactions, which all named participants have, there are three major areas of technical expertise that this work will require: (1) machine learning, statistics, molecular biophysics, and bioinformatics to build tools that integrate disparate data sources and to create predictive models (led by the Kappel Lab); (2) molecular simulations to augment existing experimental data and ground our models in biophysics (led by the Joseph Lab); and (3) deep biological expertise in both RNA-protein interactions and condensates, to guide the development of useful tools and apply them to explain and discover new biology (led by the Boeynaems Lab). Additionally, each of our aims has a large data science component that would benefit from NCEMS Staff Scientist Support. Rationale for NCEMS support: This work aligns closely with NCEMS goals: we will develop and apply tools that utilize only publicly available data; it requires close collaboration between three labs with distinct, yet complementary skills (see Rationale for working group approach); and finally, by combining our diverse scientific perspectives, we will address long-standing mysteries including how synonymous mutations and mutations in non-coding regions of RNA molecules impact cellular function, and why mutations in RNA molecules that are widely expressed have highly cell-type specific effects. Additionally, this project will require several forms of NCEMS support. First, this project requires close collaboration between three labs, located all across the country, and would benefit from the virtual leadership and team science training as well as opportunity to meet in person at the start of the project (the kickoff meeting), and the working group personnel exchange. Second, all of our proposed activities have large data science components that would benefit from NCEMS Staff Scientist Support. Third, because our labs are located at different institutions, the centralized computational and data storage resources (through CyVerse) will be critical. Requested resources Our project requires the following resources: (i) 60 TB of data storage to store all of the datasets and simulation results in a central location for the duration of the project; (ii) 1.35 million CPU hours for simulations (Model condensates made up of ~10,000 particles each running on 16 CPUs for 18 hours = 0.5 microseconds of sampling; 18 CPUs*15 hours* 2 model condensates * 2,500 mRNPs = 1.35 million CPU hours; 150 ns is adequate for equilibration, so 0.5 microsecond each should give robust statistics), access to ~8 GPUs for the duration of the project for machine learning (training and applying models); (iii) NCEMS Staff Scientist at 33% FTE for 2 years, with expertise in bioinformatics, machine learning, and statistics; (iv) NCEMS Staff Scientist Assistant at 50% FTE for 2 years, with knowledge and expertise in RNP biology, as well as basic data science skills; (v) $5000 for open-access publication costs; (vi) Travel budget for in-person kick off meeting and event coordinator to plan meeting and training events. Proposed timeline We expect that this project can be completed with 2 years of NCEMS support. Our timeline is shown in the figure below: Aim 1.1: months 1-6 Aim 2.1: months 7-12 Aim 1.2: months 7-10 Aim 2.2: months 1-6 Aim 1.3: months 7-14 Aim 2.3: months 15-21 Writing papers: months 13-24 Month: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24 We plan for several intermediate outputs, each of which we will describe in a separate open-access publication: (1) a paper describing a tool and database from Aim 1.1 and 1.2, which we will begin writing at month 13; (2) a paper describing a tool from Aim 2.1, which we will begin writing at month 13; and (3) a paper describing the applications of our tools and our biological findings from Aims 1.3 and 2.3, which we will begin writing at month 21. To make the most efficient use of the resources provided by NCEMS, and to use this project as an opportunity to train diverse early career scientists, the bulk of the work will be carried out by three teams of undergraduates, one in the Kappel Lab (green bars in timeline above), one in the Joseph Lab (blue bars), and one in the Boeynaems Lab (purple bars). The Kappel Lab undergraduate team will collaborate closely with the NCEMS Staff Scientist, the Joseph Lab undergraduate team will collaborate closely with more senior simulation experts in the Joseph Lab, and the Boeynaems Lab undergraduate team will collaborate closely with the NCEMS Staff Scientist Assistant. A staff scientist from the Boeynaems lab will also help with Aims 1.3 and 2.3. All aims will require input and discussions across all three labs — to facilitate this, we will implement bi-weekly team meetings and a dedicated Slack channel. The entire team will collaborate closely to write the manuscripts.

proposals.proposal_title: Oceans of Disorder: Elucidating the Role of Disordered Proteins in Cellular Adaptation
proposals.abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins and protein regions (collectively IDRs) are key regulators of environmental sensing, owing to their ability to undergo conformational changes in response to physicochemical fluctuations. Despite evidence from individual studies, a comprehensive understanding of IDR-driven adaptations across diverse environments remains elusive. The deep sea, characterized by extreme and variable conditions such as temperature, pressure, and salinity, offers a unique opportunity to address this knowledge gap. Over the past decade, large-scale ocean sampling expeditions using shotgun metagenomics have revolutionized our understanding of marine biodiversity, providing access to the genetic diversity of organisms, from microbes to fish, thriving in these extreme habitats. These datasets offer an unprecedented opportunity to explore how IDRs have evolved as molecular sensors to support survival across varied environmental conditions. Here, we will, for the same time, use these metagenomic datasets to systematically characterize IDRs as environmental sensors. Our multidisciplinary team, with expertise in metagenomics, protein biophysics, cell biology, and deep learning, will integrate bioinformatics, simulations, machine learning, and theoretical approaches to uncover sequence-level and functional adaptations of IDRs across marine environments. The outcomes of this research will produce a comprehensive map of IDR adaptations in marine systems, revealing their emergent properties as molecular sensors and actuators. In addition to advancing fundamental insights into stress adaptation and evolutionary biology, this work will inform biotechnological innovations, including engineering robust systems for extreme environments.
proposals.full_draft:
Introduction & goals IDRs are emerging as critical components in environmental sensing due to their unique ability to adopt dynamic conformations in response to external stimuli1. Unlike structured proteins, IDRs lack a fixed three-dimensional structure, allowing them to function as versatile molecular sensors capable of adapting to physicochemical changes2-5. While several studies have highlighted the role of IDRs in stress adaptation6-13, a systematic understanding of how IDRs enable organisms to thrive under extreme and fluctuating conditions remains a major knowledge gap. The marine environment serves as a unique natural laboratory for investigating how life adapts to variable conditions, including temperature, salinity, and pressure. The Tara Oceans project, launched in 2009, has been instrumental in advancing this understanding14,15. Over four years, using standardized protocols, Tara Oceans systematically collected over 30,000 samples from more than 200 ocean stations, including depths reaching 2,000 meters. These samples encompass various environmental conditions and yielded a vast metagenomic dataset with millions of novel sequences from viruses, prokaryotes, and eukaryotes. Analyses of this dataset have revealed temperature as a key driver of microbial community structure and uncovered previously unknown gene families3. Leveraging Tara's dataset, we will, for the first time, focus on the biophysical properties of individual proteins to uncover how they enable organisms to thrive in distinct marine environments. To achieve this, we are developing a multidisciplinary approach that integrates metagenomics, biophysical simulations, and machine learning with environmental metadata. Our project is organized around three goals: (1) Catalog and annotate IDRs: Identify IDRs in marine protein sequences and correlate their biophysical properties with environmental parameters, (2) Simulate IDR dynamics: Perform biophysical simulations of IDR dynamics under varying environmental conditions to extract key structural features, and (3) Elucidate IDR adaptation mechanisms: Establish principles of IDR adaptation by linking sequence-level features to functional biophysical properties and environmental stimuli. The outcomes of this work will address critical gaps in our understanding of IDRs functionality across diverse environments and provide a foundation for broader applications. Identifying universal principles of IDR adaptation will reveal protein plasticity mechanisms and enable the engineering of adaptable systems. Proposed activities Activity 1: Building a catalog of IDRs in marine proteins across environmental parameters We will build a comprehensive catalog of IDRs in marine proteins, correlating their biophysical properties with key environmental parameters, including temperature, salinity, and ocean depth. This work leverages the Ocean Gene Atlas v2.0 (OGA2) 16 (data source 1), a publicly available database derived from the Tara Oceans expedition, which provides extensive marine protein data. This expedition standardized sampling methodologies, collecting 12,543 samples across diverse marine ecosystems, encompassing 472 unique sampling events. These samples span a broad range of environmental conditions, including temperatures from 0 to 30 °C, ocean depths from 0 to 1000 m, and salinities between 30 to 40 PSU. 1.1: Linking marine proteins to environmental and genomic parameters. We will curate the OGA2 database, which contains approximately 45 million prokaryotic and 10 million eukaryotic protein sequences, to connect protein sequences with their environmental and genomic contexts. OGA2 includes protein abundance data and environmental metadata for each sampling location. We hypothesize that protein orthologs span diverse environments, allowing us to associate protein features with specific environmental conditions. As a proof-of-concept, we analyzed three proteins with distinct characteristics, revealing that their orthologs span a wide range of temperatures, ocean depths, and salinities (Fig. 1). Expanding on this analysis, we will systematically annotate each protein with the range of environmental conditions where it is detected. Additionally, we will link each protein to metagenome-associated genomes (MAGs) in the OceanDNA 17 database (data source 2) to incorporate genomic metadata such as genome size and GC content. 1.2: Annotating and structurally characterizing marine proteins. We will predict the structure of each protein using ESMFold 18 and AlphaFold3 19 . Domains will be identified using an integrative approach combining UniProt annotations 20 (data source 3), Chainsaw (a convolutional neural network for detection of structural domains) 21 , and Metapredict (a deep learning-based consensus predictor of IDRs) 22 . For ordered domains, we will extract detailed structural features, including secondary structures, dimensions, surface chemistry, and functional annotations where available. For disordered regions, we will extract sequence-derived features using CIDER 23 . 1.3: Labeling IDRs based on biophysical properties. IDRs will be labeled according to their intrinsic biophysical properties using ALBATROSS, a deep learning-based approach for predicting IDR ensembles under physiological conditions 24 . ALBATROSS enables assignment of properties such as radius of gyration, end-to-end distance, asphericity, Flory scaling exponent, and prefactor. Since ALBATROSS was trained for physiological conditions, its reliability may decrease under extreme conditions. To address this, we will incorporate additional biophysical labels derived from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, as outlined in Activity 2. Activity 2: Coarse-grained simulations to decipher IDR properties under different environmental conditions The functional versatility of IDRs derives from their 3D conformations, which cannot be directly inferred from their sequences 5 . These conformations are expected to adapt dynamically to environmental changes, potentially encoding mechanisms for adaptation 1 . To investigate these hypotheses, we will study IDR conformations using coarse-grained simulations under a range of environmental conditions. Specifically, we will simulate IDRs across gradients of temperature and salinity to capture their biophysical properties and structural responses. These simulations will provide detailed 3D conformational data for IDRs in marine proteins, offering insights into their adaptive mechanisms. Our approach leverages residue-level coarse-grained models that enable the efficient exploration of long timescales (up to 10s of microseconds) and larger molecular systems (up to 100,000 residues)25,26. To analyze the resulting high-dimensional data, we will integrate advanced deep learning techniques, including graph neural networks (GNNs) and variational autoencoders (VAEs), to extract structural features and annotate IDR properties. 2.1: Simulating IDRs under different environmental conditions. Building on insights from Activity 1, we will group homologous IDRs and select 1-5 representative IDRs per protein homolog to create a diverse yet focused dataset for analysis. Coarse-grained one-bead-per-residue MD simulations will be conducted for these representative IDRs. While atomistic simulations offer higher-resolution data, they are computationally prohibitive for this study. To enable extended timescale simulations and comprehensive trajectory sampling, we will employ chemically specific, residue-level coarse-grained (CG) models to simulate IDRs under specific environmental conditions: (i) salt concentration gradients using the Mpipi-Recharge model25,26; (ii) temperature gradients a custom in-house model developed by our team27. Pressure effects will not be simulated due to the absence of a validated CG model. Simulations will be performed using the open-source LAMMPS software28. We will run each IDR at three temperatures (0, 15, and 30 degrees °C) and three salt concentrations (0, 0.5, and 1M NaCl), totaling eight simulated ensembles, excluding the case near physiological conditions, which will be annotated in Activity 1.3. 2.2: Annotating biophysical properties that arise in simulations under a range of environmental conditions. We will employ deep learning-based methods to extract critical information from high-dimensional simulation data, focusing on uncovering conformational representations and structural propensities of IDRs. By leveraging advanced clustering and neural network techniques, we will learn nonlinear representations that disentangle key variation factors, capture invariant structural features, and enable the transfer of insights across diverse IDR populations. Specifically, we will integrate VAE, GNN, and generative adversarial networks to analyze MD trajectories under diverse environmental conditions29. This approach will result in an ensemble decoder that outputs multi-vector conformational matrices, highlighting key features such as global conformations, pairwise contacts, and secondary structures, which collectively annotate IDR biophysical responses. Activity 3: Mapping the mechanisms of IDR adaptation and Engineering Environmentally Resilient IDRs We will uncover the molecular principles governing the adaptation of IDRs to diverse environmental conditions. By identifying chemical features of IDRs that correlate with environmental variables (e.g., net charge variation with ocean depth), we will elucidate universal properties that can be fine-tuned to enable IDR adaptability. Comparative analyses of IDRs from orthologous proteins across different environmental contexts will reveal chemical adaptations required to maintain essential protein functions. These insights will culminate in the development of a framework for designing IDRs with enhanced adaptability and functionality tailored to specific conditions. 3.1: Identification of essential molecular features for IDR adaptation. To understand how IDRs adapt to environmental conditions, we will employ machine learning approaches to distill high-dimensional sequence and biophysical data into a low-dimensional latent space. This space will encapsulate critical features, such as compositional biases and environmentally dependent biophysical properties (e.g., radius of gyration, pairwise contacts). Key steps include: (i) Data distillation: We will train supervised or semi-supervised machine learning models to encode sequence and property data into a compact latent representation, capturing essential adaptive features. (ii) Feature mapping: By overlaying environmental parameters (e.g., temperature, salinity) onto the latent space, we will identify how IDRs modulate their features to adapt. (iii) Validation: Comparative analysis with conventional dimensionality reduction techniques (e.g., PCA, UMAP) will ensure robustness while enabling mutational and functional predictions that extend beyond conventional methods. 3.2. Predicting evolutionary trajectories and designing novel IDR sequences. Building on the insights from Activity 3.1, we will model evolutionary trajectories and design IDRs optimized for specific biophysical and environmental properties. (i) Adaptation trajectory prediction: We will use generative modeling frameworks to simulate IDR adaptation under progressive environmental conditions. These models will allow us to predict how sequence features, such as charge distribution or hydrophobicity, evolve to optimize functionality under specific conditions. We will validate predicted trajectories by comparing them to adaptation trajectories in our dataset and cross-referencing experimental data from literature or ongoing studies in related IDPs. (ii) Adaptive rule discovery: We will identify how variations in sequence features (e.g., net charge, hydropathy index) influence adaptation, enabling the formulation of "design rules" for engineering environmentally resilient IDRs. (iii) De novo sequence design: Using the latent space as a generative tool, we will design novel IDR sequences with desired biophysical properties. These sequences will be tested computationally (e.g., molecular dynamics simulations) and experimentally through collaborations with biophysics experts. This framework will enable the creation of IDPs tailored for synthetic biology and environmental resilience. Expected outcomes This research will provide transformative insights into the adaptive mechanisms of IDRs in marine proteins, elucidating their role in survival across environmental gradients such as depth, salinity, and temperature. By cataloging IDRs alongside their biophysical properties and environmental metadata, we will establish the first comprehensive database linking IDR biophysical features to environmental contexts. This database will serve as a foundational resource for understanding the evolutionary adaptations of IDRs. Through large-scale simulations and machine learning models, we expect to uncover universal chemical features that govern IDR adaptability. These findings will address critical knowledge gaps and provide a foundation for engineering environmentally adaptable proteins. The resulting tools and frameworks will have broad applicability, extending beyond marine systems to other biological contexts, and paving the way for advances in synthetic biology, biotechnology, and evolutionary studies. We anticipate at least four publishable outcomes from this work: (i) A database of marine IDRs cataloging sequence features and environmental metadata, (ii) Large-scale simulations and biophysical analyses revealing key adaptive features, (iii) A machine learning-based predictor of IDR adaptation pathways, and (iv) A computational tool for the de novo design of IDRs tailored to specific environmental niches. These outputs will empower team members to take ownership of distinct project aspects while fostering collaborations. Moreover, the dataset will lay the groundwork for experimental studies to validate predictions and develop innovative approaches for engineering IDRs. This integrative effort will catalyze progress in designing robust, environmentally adaptable proteins, pushing the boundaries of synthetic biology and evolutionary studies. Rationale for the working group collaborative approach The scope and interdisciplinary demands of this project are beyond what a single lab can address alone. Understanding the interactions between IDR sequence, structure, and function across diverse environments requires expertise in multiple disciplines, including metagenomics, biophysics, and machine learning. By combining these skill sets, our working group provides a unique platform to tackle the project's challenges effectively: (i) Metagenomics and bioinformatics: Experts will curate and analyze large datasets of marine proteins, annotate IDRs with environmental and genomic parameters, and uncover adaptation trends. This work establishes a foundation for identifying patterns of IDR adaptation across ecosystems. (ii) Biophysics and modeling: These experts will utilize advanced simulation tools, many developed by members of the working group. These tools are essential for modeling IDR behavior under diverse environmental conditions, offering unparalleled insights into conformational dynamics and adaptation mechanisms. Their expertise is foundational to the project, deepening our understanding of how IDRs function and evolve across varying contexts. (iii) Machine Learning: These experts will apply advanced algorithms to analyze high-dimensional molecular dynamics data, extracting otherwise inaccessible structural and functional insights. Their contributions will enable predictive modeling and the design of novel, environmentally adaptable IDRs. By combining these areas of expertise, our working group fosters innovation and ensures the creation of broadly applicable tools and frameworks. Rationale for NCEMS support This project requires NCEMS support and resources because its scope and complexity extend beyond the capabilities of a single lab or existing collaborations. NCEMS's unique infrastructure and expertise make it an ideal partner to address the following critical needs: (i) Simulation management: Processing and analyzing approximately 440,000 MD trajectories demands specialized computational support and infrastructure. NCEMS provides the necessary CPU hours and data management resources to ensure efficient processing and high-quality results. (ii) Database development: Building a comprehensive database that catalogs IDRs, integrates biophysical properties, and links them to environmental metadata requires expertise in database design, curation, and integration of diverse datasets. NCEMS offers the tools and expertise to create such a robust and scalable database. (iii) Collaborative environment: The project's multidisciplinary nature—spanning metagenomics, biophysics, computational modeling, and machine learning— necessitates an environment that fosters seamless collaboration between experts from diverse fields. NCEMS's infrastructure is designed to facilitate this type of interdisciplinary synergy, ensuring efficient coordination and innovation. (iv) AI expertise: Extracting meaningful connections between IDR sequences, environmental factors, and adaptation mechanisms requires advanced deep learning capabilities. NCEMS's access to AI experts will enable the development of novel predictive models, providing transformative insights that would be difficult to achieve otherwise. By addressing these challenges, NCEMS support will ensure the project's success, catalyzing breakthroughs in our understanding of IDR-driven adaptation and enabling the development of innovative tools with broad applicability. Requested resources We request the following resources to accomplish the project's objectives: (i) 33% FTE Staff Scientist: The staff scientist will collaborate with the group to design and build the IDR catalog, develop advanced data analysis strategies, and identify relationships between IDR behaviors and environmental conditions. This position requires expertise in bioinformatics and data analysis to ensure the project's scientific goals are met effectively. (ii) 50% FTE Staff Scientist Assistant: The assistant will manage and curate the extensive MD simulations critical for processing the estimated 416,000 MD trajectories while ensuring data quality and throughput. Additionally, they will support the group in establishing infrastructure to create a seamless and collaborative environment among team members, enhancing productivity and integration. (iii) CPU Hours: OGA2 includes approximately 45 million prokaryotic proteins and 10 million eukaryotic proteins. Based on IDR predictors, an estimated 5% of prokaryotic proteins and 30% of eukaryotic proteins contain IDRs30. After filtering for redundancy, such as same-species occurrences and close orthologs, we estimate the need to simulate approximately 22,000 prokaryotic proteins with IDRs averaging 80 amino acids (AA) in length and 30,000 eukaryotic proteins with IDRs averaging 150 AA. Each simulation will run for 5 microseconds. Given that simulation time scales with the square of the number of amino acids, our benchmarks indicate that simulating an 80-residue IDR requires 6.4 hours (equivalent to 25.6 CPU hours), while simulating a 150-residue IDR requires 22.5 hours (equivalent to 90 CPU hours). Based on these calculations, we estimate a total of 3,263,200 CPU hours per condition. With eight conditions to simulate, the project will require approximately 26,105,600 CPU hours. These computational resources are crucial for integrating computational, theoretical, and experimental approaches, enabling the team to address complex challenges, achieve transformative outcomes, and advance NCEMS's mission of fostering community-scale synthesis and innovation. (iv) Data Storage Requirements: Analysis of the OGA2 dataset will require approximately 1 TB to accommodate both processed and raw data. Extracting genomic data from the OceanDNA resource to provide genomic properties will require an additional 8 TB. For Activity 2, each 5-microsecond MD simulation generates approximately 100 MB of data, including input and output files. With a total of 416,000 simulations planned, this will necessitate 42 TB of storage. Altogether, the project requires 52 TB of storage to ensure seamless integration of computational, theoretical, and experimental approaches, enabling the generation of transformative insights into IDR adaptation. Proposed Timeline The proposed 24-month timeline is designed to ensure the successful completion of the project's interdisciplinary goals, aligning with the complexity and scope of each aim. Activity 1 (first 6 months): The initial phase will focus on designing and building the IDR catalog by annotating and integrating marine protein datasets with their associated environmental metadata. This foundational step will involve data curation, initial analyses, and collaboration between metagenomics and bioinformatics team members, supported by the requested staff scientist and computational resources from NCEMS. Activity 2 (months 5–16): Over 12 months, the team will run and curate MD simulations for the cataloged IDRs, processing approximately 440,000 MD trajectories. This phase will require substantial computational resources and dedicated staff to manage data quality. Advanced data analysis strategies will be developed to identify key relationships between IDR behaviors and environmental conditions. We will publish preliminary findings from the simulation data during this phase, ensuring early dissemination of key results to the scientific community. Activity 3 (year two): The second year will leverage the results from the MD simulations to develop machine learning models and predictive tools for IDR adaptation pathways. This phase will also focus on designing de novo IDRs tailored to specific environmental and functional demands. Initially, the team will derive correlations and conclusions from datasets without MD simulations to establish baseline insights. These findings will then be expanded by incorporating the trajectory data as a second step, allowing for deeper and more comprehensive analyses. Additionally, we will publish final project outcomes, ensuring results are disseminated within the project timeline.
