proposals.proposal_title: Multimodel single-cell frameworks for cell lines with extensive multi-omics data
proposals.abstract: Large-scale consortia like the Dependency Map and Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia have generated extensive multi-omics data for over 2000 primary cell lines, including bulk measurements of DNA, chromatin accessibility, RNA, and proteins. Recently, multi-omics single-cell sequencing and imaging data labeling RNA and proteins for these cell lines have become increasingly available. However, these datasets remain fragmented, lacking integration into a unified framework to model and quantify DNA, RNA, and protein within the same cell. While previous efforts have created multimodal benchmark datasets, these often include diverse samples from multiple donors and heterogeneous cell types. In contrast, our project focuses on single model systems, such as commonly used cell lines, which already feature extensive single-cell, bulk sequencing, and imaging data. By eliminating donor and cell type variability, our approach enables robust analyses and precise alignment across modalities, including RNA, protein, and chromatin accessibility. This focus on homogenous cell types within a consistent biological context facilitates mechanistic studies of regulatory interactions and perturbation responses, minimizing confounding variability. We aim to develop multimodal frameworks for 7 cell lines and computational pipelines to analyze relationships across DNA, RNA, and protein levels. By incorporating additional multi-omics data, including bulk and single-cell perturbation datasets (e.g., loss-of-function screens and Perturb-seq), we will create a comprehensive benchmarking resource. With expertise in machine learning, network biology, and genomics, and NCEMS support for data wrangling, our team will deliver tools to study regulatory mechanisms and cellular resource allocation. These efforts will foster fundamental discoveries, community-driven resource development, and innovation in multi-omics research.

proposals.proposal_title: From image data and biophysical simulations to principles of mesoscale organization through integrated transfer learning
proposals.abstract: Mesoscale cellular organization emerges from complex interactions among chemical, structural, and physical components. Understanding how mesoscale structures influence local and collective cellular properties remains a significant challenge, often beyond the scope of individual experimental studies. While vast image datasets for cellular components exist, their full potential for deeper secondary analysis and synthesis remains untapped. We propose to synthesize morphological and physico-chemical measurements from cell image, in vitro, and in silico data to unravel the principles of mesoscale cellular organization. Our approach will develop a pipeline using transfer learning and mutual prediction, trained on complete datasets (all components of interest present) and applied to incomplete datasets (missing one or more components). This methodology will uncover relationships between cellular components and enable holistic systems-level predictions. To demonstrate the generalizability and biological relevance of this approach, we will test it on three increasingly complex mesoscale systems centered on the nucleus: (1) nucleus-nucleolus, (2) nucleus-centrosome-microtubules, and (3) nucleus-mitochondria-mitochondrial condensates. These test cases will showcase how our method integrates and predicts complex systems relationships, advancing our understanding of mesoscale cellular organization.
proposals.full_draft: Background Understanding mesoscale cellular organization requires investigating the interplay of physical forces, spatial constraints, and interactions between cellular components. Advances in morphological profiling, spatial and organellar proteomics, and generative whole-cell modeling have laid the foundation for mapping organizational patterns on scales ranging from molecules to organelles. However, achieving a holistic view of what drives mesoscale organization necessitates integrating these components across each other and with biophysical principles. This proposal shifts focus from traditional gene/protein-centric views to explore how physical principles and geometric constraints give rise to cellular architecture. By combining existing cell imaging data, in vitro reconstitution of mesoscale structures, and published outcomes of molecular simulations, we aim to develop a framework to predict how cellular architectures emerge from the localization, morphology, and interactions of components. This integrative approach will uncover emergent behaviors and previously unidentified features in high-dimensional datasets. Quantitative comparisons across high-dimensional datasets are challenging due to differences in data space. Traditional methods like clustering require data to reside in a single space, but advances in metric geometry, particularly Gromov-Wasserstein distances, enable comparisons across distinct spaces. Recent applications of GW distances have demonstrated their utility in aligning single-cell data and comparing biological networks and time-series data. Here, we propose leveraging GW distances to develop transfer learning algorithms to integrate biological datasets of mesoscale structures. This approach addresses critical gaps in cross-space learning, enabling rigorous integrative analyses of multimodal data. Driving Questions How much of mesoscale cell organization arises from intrinsic physical properties of structures versus their interactions? What role do mesoscale interactions play in determining the morphological and physico-chemical properties of cytoskeletal, organelle, and condensate components? Can a transfer learning approach infer morphological and physical properties of mesoscale structures from joint and incomplete datasets to address these questions and beyond? Proposed Activities Generalizable computational analysis and modeling approach Our approach integrates multicomponent image data to predict unseen properties in incomplete datasets. We extract high-dimensional morphological feature sets describing component size, shape, number, position, and inter-component interactions. Dynamic metrics, such as positional and shape changes, are included for live-cell data. Dimensional reduction generates interpretable feature spaces, which can be tuned for exploratory or hypothesis-driven studies, including granular dissection of cross-component interdependencies and contextual comparisons such as drug treatments, disease states, and cell types. The feature space is sampled along statistical dimensions to reveal feature covariance and specific feature evolutions. Using GW distance analysis to go beyond by-eye interpretations, we quantitatively describe feature covariance and predictive relationships between components. This two-step approach integrates and learns from data across cellular contexts: Step 1: Integrate data across cells. Multicomponent images are aligned via GW distances, generating pairwise similarity matrices for features of interest. This enables comparisons across distinct data spaces, leveraging complex features such as organelle shape. Step 2: Infer feature relationships. Deep learning on alignment matrices reveals predictive relationships between features. Generative adversarial networks under GW distance and transfer learning algorithms facilitate inference, validated using open-source datasets. To tackle the complexity of cellular data, we will incorporate data from minimal systems to compare intrinsic properties in isolated components versus cellular contexts and test whether morphology predicts physical or chemical properties. These data reveal the intrinsic properties of the component in isolation, providing a baseline for comparison with the cellular context. Morphological and physical feature spaces extracted from in vitro and in silico data will be compared with cell image features. New simulations will be developed to ask whether inter-component interactions could close the gap between minimal system and cellular feature distributions. If not, this could indicate that other interactors or environmental factors need to be incorporated. Translating images, which are high-dimensional representations of reality, into physical models requires a combination of approaches. First, we analyze images to extract the underlying physics using low-dimensional models. Second, GW distance analysis can form the basis for standard granular agent-based models. We aim to develop physical models alongside molecular and cellular descriptions to identify mechanisms governing complex processes. Application of workflow to test cases We will refine our workflow by applying it to three mesoscale interaction systems: Nucleus and Nucleolus. Integration of image and minimal system data will explore universal principles governing nucleolar morphology, dynamics, and chromatin interactions. In vitro and simulation data for nucleoli revealing biophysical properties such as surface tension and fluidity will be incorporated. Nucleus, centrosome, and microtubules. This system spans membrane-bound, condensate, and cytoskeletal components. Using multicomponent imaging datasets, we will reconstruct three-part feature relationships from two-component feature relationships and validate findings with in vitro data for microtubules and centrosome. The visibility of all three components in tubulin staining patterns will be leveraged to predict missing components from single-component images. Mitochondria, mitochondrial nucleoids, and nucleus. We examine how morphological properties of mitochondrial nucleoids, which behave as biomolecular condensates, are related to mitochondrial and nuclear structure and function. High-throughput imaging of fibroblasts from healthy and HGPS patients, where mitochondrial nucleoid morphology is altered, will reveal links between structural changes and cellular aging and enable prediction of mitochondrial nucleoid properties in other images. Integration and Synthesis The nucleus serves as an anchor point across test cases due to its extensive biological characterization and rich representation across multicomponent and minimal system data types. After initial workflow implementation, findings will be integrated into a larger model incorporating all components across test cases with the nucleus at the nexus, revealing new mesoscale interactions. Limitations in dataset availability, findability, and quality will likely necessitate further data scouting, particularly for in vitro and in silico data. Systematic literature synthesis methods adapted from the interdisciplinary community will provide complementary insights, building on novel applications for fundamental cell biology currently under development by Mary Mirvis. This combined approach will give insight into variability and reproducibility of findings, supporting robust statistical analyses and modeling efforts. Outcomes The project will yield key outcomes aimed at advancing our understanding of mesoscale cellular organization. These include: a generalizable analytical framework, a computational pipeline leveraging GW distances and transfer learning to analyze multicomponent imaging datasets; predictive models validated for inferring unseen properties from incomplete datasets; integrated datasets combining cell image, in vitro, and in silico sources; and new biophysical insights into mesoscale structure-function relationships spanning sub-nucleus dynamics, organelle interactions, and cytoskeletal organization. Broader Impacts By enabling the integration of diverse datasets, the project will facilitate systems-level analyses of cellular organization and dynamic processes. The generalizable methods will benefit disciplines ranging from biophysics to computational biology. Additionally, by providing new tools and datasets, the work will empower researchers to explore previously intractable mesoscale and multiscale cellular organization questions. Rationale for a Working Group Approach The proposed work requires expertise in computational image analysis, statistical and mathematical modeling including machine learning and simulations, biological and biophysical insight into specific test cases, and deep subject matter expertise for meaningful interpretation of results. No single lab possesses all of these qualities, but our group includes field leaders in all relevant fields. A multi-lab collaboration also expands access to additional complete and well-documented datasets, enhancing the robustness and impact of our analyses. Rationale for NCEMS Support Our proposal builds on several open-source data and methods resources and aims to produce an open-source, highly generalizable data integration workflow to benefit the scientific community, strongly in line with NCEMS’ mission. We will require IT support from NCEMS due to the computational demands of GW distance analyses, which are computationally expensive. Additionally, high-resolution image data necessitates substantial data storage resources, another area where NCEMS can provide critical support. Furthermore, this project involves extensive data and knowledge synthesis, including the integration of image datasets and feature data from dynamic and static cell images, in vitro studies, and simulations, as well as comprehensively synthesized published findings. NCEMS support can enhance these efforts by facilitating systematic curation and pooling of smaller datasets, assembling a large, diverse corpus. These efforts address gaps in publicly available resources, enabling broader applications of the pipeline. Requested Resources We expect to use TensorFlow and PyTorch to train deep learning models and the POT Python library to compute GW distances. For each instance of model training, we expect approximately two hours of training time per GPU, with total time depending on the need to train additional models. Initially, we estimate requiring at least ten thousand GPU hours, with this demand scaling proportionally as additional datasets are integrated into the analysis. High-resolution imaging datasets and intermediate data products, including simulation outputs, will require substantial storage capacity, estimated at approximately fifty terabytes for the duration of the project. Assistance from NCEMS and CYVERSE IT specialists will be critical for optimizing workflows, managing data transfers, and ensuring compatibility between datasets and computational tools. As part of the project’s data synthesis efforts, we also require support for systematic dataset curation and integration, including scouting and pooling smaller datasets from literature and open-source repositories. Proposed Timeline A two-year timeline is appropriate for the proposed work. Development of the core workflow for cell image feature space comparison for two-component test cases is expected to take at least six months. Further refinement, expansion to three-component systems, incorporation of additional data types, and integration across test cases will extend through the second year, depending on availability of data, resources, and personnel.

proposals.proposal_title: Transposable elements and the emergence of genomic innovation
proposals.abstract: Our working group aims to comprehensively investigate how transposable elements (TEs) contribute to genomic innovation and species diversification in vertebrates through the generation of novel functional elements. While TEs comprise nearly half of the human genome and are increasingly recognized as sources of regulatory innovation, their repetitive nature has complicated their analysis using short-read sequencing technologies. We propose a two-phase approach: First, we will reprocess tens of thousands of publicly available genomic datasets (including ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, RNA-seq, and Ribo-seq) using repeat-aware analysis pipelines and new telomere-to-telomere and pangenome assemblies. Second, we will synthesize this reprocessed data to understand how TEs generate new transcription factor binding sites, cell-specific and species-specific enhancers, novel transcripts, and protein-coding sequences. The project combines multidisciplinary expertise from multiple labs and will leverage advanced computational approaches to uncover complex relationships between TEs and regulatory networks. Our investigation represents a quintessential mesoscale emergence phenomenon, bridging molecular-level TE insertions with emergent regulatory networks and phenotypic innovations. The project will produce both a comprehensive public data resource of repeat-aware genomic analyses and new insights into how TEs drive biological innovation through regulatory network evolution.
proposals.full_draft:
Introduction Transposable elements (TE) are mobile genetic elements that can paste themselves into new genomic locations, thereby resulting in the duplication of DNA. Almost half of the human genome is derived from TE transposition activity 1. Since their discovery by Barbara McClintock almost 80 years ago, the biological and evolutionary roles of TE-derived DNA have been contentiously debated2,3. While they were previously dismissed as “selfish genetic elements” and “junk DNA”, it is now becoming clear that TEs play key roles in the evolutionary diversification of organisms by serving as the raw material for novel functional genomic elements. For example, a recent estimate suggests that over 85% of primate-specific transcription factor (TF) binding sites are derived from TEs 4. Thus, it might be said that TEs are largely responsible for what makes us human. Unfortunately, the repetitive nature of TEs has made it difficult to characterize their functional roles using sequencing-based genomic assays. Popular genomics assays for characterizing regulatory elements (ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, DNase-seq), transcription (RNA-seq, TT-seq), and translation (Ribo-seq) have typically relied on high-throughput short-read sequencing platforms. The first step in analyzing these data is mapping the sequenced reads back to their source genomic locations. However, shorter sequencing read lengths give rise to “multi-mapped” reads (MMRs) that align equally well to multiple genomic locations. Most regulatory genomics analysis pipelines discard MMRs or assign them randomly 5. Since multi-mapped reads arise predominantly from repetitive regions of the genome, current analysis pipelines fail to detect a substantial portion of functional events that occur in repetitive regions. Using the common read lengths (35-100bp) seen in many studies and public repositories, up to 30% of sequenced reads are not uniquely mappable 6 (Figure 1). Therefore, TEs and other repetitive regions have been largely overlooked in most regulatory genomics analyses. Despite the analysis challenges, recent studies present overwhelming evidence that TEs play a crucial role in generating novel genomic elements. Several studies have demonstrated that TEs generate new TF binding sites, suggesting that they play active roles in gene regulation 4,7,8. The Zoonomia consortium showed that over 20% of all TF binding sites in the human genome, including 85% of primate-specific sites, were derived from transposable elements (TEs) 4. Recent results from working group member Ting Wang demonstrated that TE-derived regulatory elements show similar enhancer activity and GWAS variant enrichment to non-TE-derived elements 9 . TEs have also been implicated in the evolution of mammalian pregnancy development 10 , interferon response 11 , and pluripotency maintenance 12 . TE mobilization has also been shown to perturb gene regulation and create disease states such as breast cancer 13 . A pair of recent studies suggests that TEs can also serve as a source of novel species-specific protein coding sequences 14,15 . Most of these studies did not properly account for multi-mapped reads in their analyses, typically only investigating older TE-derived elements that are uniquely mappable. Thus, the representation of TEs and other repetitive elements in biological processes is likely under-characterized. To fully understand how TEs lead to the generation of novel functional elements in the genome, we need to use analysis approaches that fully account for MMRs. Several methods have been proposed to handle MMRs in regulatory genomics data 16–27 . They follow two types of approaches, both of which are valuable. The first set of approaches finds family-level associations between regulatory genomics signals and repeat element classes, for example by mapping reads to TE family consensus sequences 20,21 . The recent T3E tool exemplifies this family-level approach 21 . Another set of approaches aims to probabilistically allocate MMRs in the genome by using uniquely mapped read counts in the vicinity of possible MMR mapping locations 16,17,19,28 . For example, the Mahony lab has recently developed Allo 28 , which is easily integrated into existing regulatory genomics pipelines and which provides superior MMR allocation accuracy. In a preliminary analysis, we used Allo to reprocess 481 ENCODE TF ChIP-seq datasets from the human K562 cell line. Incorporating Allo led to the discovery of 385,563 new TF binding sites in this data collection, compared with the standard ENCODE pipeline that does not properly account for MMRs (Figure 2A). Allo is particularly effective at enabling the discovery of TF binding sites in young (primate-specific) TE families such as SVA and ERVK elements (Figure 2B). Finally, newly available genome assemblies provide unprecedented resolution of repetitive regions in the genome. The human and mouse Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) projects provided complete assemblies that fill in the gaps over highly repetitive regions such as centromeres, telomeres, tandem repeat arrays, and segmental duplications 29 . New pangenome graph assemblies provide representation of structural variation and TE insertions in the human population 30–33 . Short sequencing reads can be more accurately aligned against both T2T and pangenome assemblies, compared with the reference genomes 30,34 . Thus, these new genome assemblies provide a timely opportunity to reevaluate the functional roles of TEs. Goals In this proposed NCEMS Working Group, our overall goal is to understand how TEs contribute to novel functional elements that drive evolutionary diversification of vertebrate phenotypes. We will do this by synthesizing several layers of regulatory genomics, transcriptomics, and ribosome profiling data that will be reprocessed using repeat-aware analysis pipelines, and by integrating analyses across data modalities, cell types, and species. Biological questions: Our proposed large-scale reprocessing of epigenomic data collections will enable us to tackle the following biological questions. Answering each of these questions will require integrative data synthesis across data types, across cell types, and/or across vertebrate species. 1. How do TEs generate new TF binding sites? a. How many species-specific (e.g., human-specific) TF binding sites are TE-derived? b. Do particular TFs favor the binding of particular TE families? 2. What is the role of TEs in generating novel cell-specific enhancers? a. How do enhancer chromatin state signatures vary across cell types? b. Do TE families preferentially display enhancer signatures in particular cell types? 3. What is the role of TEs in generating novel species-specific enhancers? a. Which TE families generate enhancers in different vertebrate species? b. Do species-specific TE expansions generate novel tissue-specific enhancers? 4. How do TEs contribute to the generation of novel transcripts? 5. How do TEs contribute to the generation of novel protein-coding sequences? Proposed activities Phase 1: Reprocessing regulatory genomics data collections with repeat-aware pipelines During the initial phase of the project, we will work with NCEMS staff scientists to reprocess tens of thousands of publicly available regulatory genomics datasets using repeat-aware analysis approaches. Specifically, we will download and reprocess all ATAC-seq (bulk and single-cell), DNase-seq, TF ChIP-seq, histone ChIP-seq, RNA-seq (bulk and single-cell), and Ribo-seq data from several well-annotated, publicly available collections. We will reprocess both human and mouse data collections from the ENCODE consortium, human data from the NIH Roadmap Epigenomics consortium, agricultural species (cow, pig, and chicken) data from the Functional Annotation of Animal Genomes (FAANG) consortium, and selected human and primate expression data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) consortium. We will source human, mouse, and rat Ribo-seq data from the SRA with annotations from the RiboSeq Data Portal. Appropriate analysis pipelines that incorporate repeat-aware analysis steps will be applied to each data modality. Human and mouse data will be aligned to the new, complete “Telomere-to-Telomere” genome assemblies 30,35, which provide greatly improved characterization of highly repetitive regions of the genome. In parallel, human data will also be aligned to the draft human pangenome graph assembly 30 . ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and DNase-seq will be aligned using bowtie2 36 (T2T assemblies) and vg map 37 (pangenome assemblies) with settings that keep up to 50 read mapping locations per read. T3E will be applied to generate TE-family associations for each signal 21. Allo will be used to probabilistically allocate MMRs to individual mapping locations, after which peak-finding will be performed using MACS2 38. RNA-seq and Ribo-seq will be aligned using STAR 39 with settings that keep up to 50 read mapping locations per read. Rcount 23 and Allo will then be used to probabilistically allocate reads. Read counts will be quantified for known transcripts (using GENCODE annotations 40), novel transcripts (assembled using StringTie2 41), and TEs. Importantly, all proposed data analysis tools exist and are fully tested. No new tool development is required. Rather, NCEMS will be asked to assist with modifying existing analysis pipelines and to execute these pipelines at scale via CyVerse computational resources. The targeted data collections are well-annotated and easily accessible. Thus, this phase of the project is “shovel ready” for execution. Phase 2: Data synthesis to understand the role of TEs in generating novel functional elements Our working group will leverage the repeat-aware data collection established in Phase 1 to study TE-derived functional elements. Phase 2 will focus on answering the biological questions outlined under the Goals section above. We will start by defining TE-derived TF binding sites, transcripts, and translated sequences by overlapping with RepeatMasker annotations. Species-specific and lineage-specific elements will be defined by assessing their conservation via Zoonomia 241-species multi-way alignments 4. We will use hidden Markov model approaches to annotate chromatin states in different cell types and species using the reprocessed histone modification ChIP-seq and chromatin accessibility data types 42,43. This will provide an annotation of potential TE-derived enhancers and other regulatory regions. Associations between TE families, TFs, expressed sequences, cell types, and species will be assessed using statistical enrichment analyses. Beyond straightforward association-based analyses, we will also perform cross-cutting, integrative analyses across the data collection to uncover hidden connections between data modalities. Specifically, we will apply tensor decomposition approaches to find links between components of the dataset. This approach has the potential to uncover complex interdependencies within the dataset. It could, for instance, highlight cases where a particular set of TFs are driving enhancer activities in a class of TEs that in turn have an impact on a tissue-specific gene expression program. Phase 2 will culminate in the collation of results and manuscript writing. Outcomes Phase 1 will result in a comprehensive compendium of regulatory genomics, transcriptomics, and ribosome profiling datasets that have been consistently reprocessed to measure regulatory activities and expression at repeat elements. In adherence with open science principles, processed data (alignment BAM files, ChIP-seq peaks, expression tables, etc.) will be made publicly available, empowering new research by illuminating genomic regions that are normally “masked”. We will also share our data analysis pipelines to ensure transparency and reproducibility. Phase 2 will result in a collaborative research publication describing the outcomes of our integrative data analyses. Working group members will also draft a review-style article describing the current bestpractices for repeat-aware processing of regulatory genomics data. Rationale for a working group approach Our proposed working group assembles a unique combination of experts who share a common interest in how TEs generate novel genomic elements, but who are each focused on distinct layers of biological activities and who are each bringing complementary analysis approaches. The NCEMS working group offers a unique opportunity to bring these diverse interests and approaches together to gain a comprehensive understanding of how TEs drive genomic novelty and species diversification. Specifically, we will bring together leading experts in the functionalization of TE-derived elements (Wang, Chuong) with experts in TE evolution (Ray, Konkel), regulatory element evolution (Hardison), evolution of novel protein-coding sequences (Carvunis), inference of cell type specific TE activity using single-cell omics (Subramanian), and machine learning approaches for regulatory genomics data (Mahony, Whalley). In addition, the computational resources required to pursue the proposed project are beyond the resources available to individual labs. As outlined in the requested resources section, we anticipate reprocessing over 75,000 regulatory genomics experiments. Our preliminary analysis of approximately 1% of these data took several weeks to process using our locally available computational resources. Rationale for NCEMS support Our proposed working group is highly compatible with the goals of the NCEMS. We aim to catalyze a multidisciplinary team of scientists to synthesize publicly available data to address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biosciences: How do TEs contribute to genomic innovation? Our central goal combines two of the longest-standing puzzles in molecular biology: 1) Do TEs play functional roles?; and 2) How do regulatory networks adapt to generate novel phenotypes and behaviors across species? The evolution of regulatory networks through TE-derived regulatory elements is a quintessential example of a mesoscale emergence phenomenon as it bridges multiple biological scales. At its foundation are molecular-level TE insertion events, which create new potential regulatory elements and expressed sequences that become incorporated into existing networks. The emergent properties manifest as new tissue-specific expression patterns that could not be predicted from individual components alone, while the effects span multiple biological scales from DNA sequence changes through regulatory networks up to phenotypic innovations. This embodies the mesoscale concept of understanding how lower-level molecular changes manifest as higher-level biological phenomena. Requested resources • NCEMS Staff Scientist: 8 months support over 2 years (6 mo. in Year 1; 2 mo. in Year 2) • NCEMS Staff Scientist Assistant: 50% FTE in each of two years. • Computational resources: 10M CPU hours. • Travel budget: funds requested to support in-person meeting at the start of the initiative. • Project manager and event coordinator support as necessary to goals of project. • Publication costs: $5,000 to support open access publication fees in Year 2. • Personnel exchange costs: funds requested to support two short-term graduate student exchanges between labs in Year 2. Proposed timeline We request two years of NCEMS support. Each of the two project phases outlined in the proposed activities will be approximately one year in duration. Year 1 (Phase 1 activities, Phase 2 planning): We will begin by gathering representatives of all working group labs for a 2-day in-person jamboree meeting at Penn State’s University Park campus. During this meeting, we will finalize data analysis plans, including specifying the details of analysis pipelines for each targeted data modality. Immediately following the jamboree, we will work with an NCEMS Staff Scientist to implement and execute the proposed data reanalysis pipelines (expected commitment: 6 months). While Phase 1 data processing is ongoing, we will schedule virtual working group meetings every two weeks (facilitated by an NCEMS Project Manager) to plan the details of Phase 2 activities. An NCEMS Staff Scientist Assistant (expected commitment: 6 months, 50% FTE) will implement Phase 2 analysis pipelines as they are approved by the working group, ensuring that the Phase 2 analysis pipelines will be ready to execute at the completion of Phase 1. Year 2 (Phase 2 activities, publication drafting): An NCEMS Staff Scientist will implement and execute the Phase 2 analysis pipelines across all reprocessed regulatory genomics datasets (expected commitment: 2 months). The working group will continue to meet virtually every two weeks, and discussions will focus on the results of Phase 2 synthesis & analysis. Working group members will gather and interpret the results of Phase 2 pipelines and an NCEMS Staff Scientist Assistant will implement and execute additional follow-up analyses at the direction of the working group (expected commitment: 6 months, 50% FTE). Working group members will collaboratively write a research manuscript describing both the NCEMS-generated data resource and the results of our integrative synthesis analyses. Working group members will also draft a review article outlining current approaches for studying TE-derived functional elements and describing outstanding challenges in the field.

proposals.proposal_title: Searching the crosslinking mass spectrometry universe for new protein-protein interactions
proposals.abstract: Crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) is a powerful structural proteomics method that can provide high-resolution structural information about complex mixtures of proteins in their native physiological context.1,2,3 The method works by chemically crosslinking two reactive amino acid residues that are close to one another in 3-D space, thereby freezing this spatial information into a covalent bond, and then retrieving this information by sequencing crosslinked peptides following enzymatic digest of the constituent proteins (like Hi-C,4 but for proteins). Initially developed in the 2000s to interrogate purified proteins, by the late-2010s, methods became available to interrogate protein-protein interactions (PPIs) on the proteome-scale and in the cellular environment.5 This project seeks to standardize, combine, and integrate existing publicly available crosslinking datasets from PRIDE to make these data more re-usable and useful for integrative and hybrid modeling. We will also create a meta-dataset to catalogue PPIs in human and other model organisms. Because XL-MS encodes information about both protein identity and interacting residues, these findings can be cross-validated to structural predictions of protein complexes using AlphaFold3, thereby providing stronger evidence for their existence compared to huMAP3.0, which predicts protein complexes without structural evidence. We will integrate these findings into the EBI Complex Portal to make it accessible to the life science community.
proposals.full_draft:
4. Introduction: Every protein is connected.6 The physical interactions made by proteins oftentimes define their functions; hence, to understand the whole proteome, we must also have a complete compendium of protein complexes. Several proteomics approaches can be used to infer the existence of a pairwise protein-protein interaction (the fundamental unit of data used to build a model of a protein complex), such as affinity purification mass spectrometry (AP-MS), proximity labeling,7 co-fractionation mass spectrometry (CF-MS),8 and PAR-CL-MS (photoactivated RNA crosslinked coupled to mass spectrometry).9 BioPlex3.0 represents a particularly large-scale effort to catalogue human protein complexes,10 since the project’s inception in 2015,11 now 17,000 separate AP-MS experiments have been conducted by individually epitope-tagging nearly every human protein and then detecting which other proteins co-purify with it. huMAP3.0 combines BioPlex3.0 with data from CF-MS and proximity labeling and uses a machine learning model to cluster the PPI pairs into a global PPI network.12 This network estimates there to be 15,000 complexes in the human proteome and that 14,000 proteins in the human proteome exist in some complex. These predictions were recently incorporated into the EBI Complex Portal, greatly expanding the 2,150 manually curated human protein complexes.13,14 Whilst AP-MS, proximity labeling, and CF-MS are powerful methods, none of them provide structural information or evidence of which residues/interfaces are involved in a PPI. Moreover, AP-MS and CF- MS require that a complex survive lysis and remain intact in vitro, which means that they cannot generally capture proteins that are transiently associated with a complex. Crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) is an orthogonal method for interrogating protein interactions that encodes a PPI by sequencing the two peptides derived from the two separate proteins covalently connected to each other through a chemical crosslinker (Figure 1A). Originally conceived as a structural method to be applied to purified proteins in vitro, advancements in crosslinker technology (i.e., MS-cleavable crosslinkers), mass spec instrumentation (i.e., high mass accuracy, sensitivity, and speed), and search software have enabled XL-MS to be applied to proteome-wide samples (Figure 1B).5 In other words, a contact between any reactive residue X on any protein A to any reactive residue Y on any protein B can be sequenced. For a number of years, confidently identifying an inter-protein crosslink in a proteome-wide sample was considered very challenging, particularly because the search software did not have the capacity to estimate the FDR properly. 15,16,17 This challenge has largely been overcome, and new algorithms (like Scout 18 ) can perform these searches and validations quickly. The XL-MS community has, in general, been amenable to making raw data available on PRIDE, one of the member repositories of the ProteomExchange. Currently, there are ~1000 such datasets. However, it is not easy for these data to be reused or integrated for numerous reasons: (1) Over the years, many different search algorithms have been used, with various strengths and weaknesses (some are quite problematic); (2) Many experiments use customized fasta databases or search method parameters; (3) Until recently, there was not a unified format for reporting processed data (such as lists of residue-residue pairs), hence they were deposited to PRIDE as “partial crosslinking submissions”; (4) Sample metadata regarding tissue type, cell line, or disease conditions are often poorly annotated, posing significant challenges in linking the structure and complex to specific phenotypes or cellular molecular states. This project has three proposed activities. Firstly, it aims to select large-scale XL-MS data in the PRIDE Archive, re-annotate them using SDRF (Sample and Data Relationship Format 19 ) and reanalyze them using modern search algorithms, so that their findings can be more trustworthy and more readily reused by computational structural biologists. Secondly, it aims to mine through those data to (a) search for potentially new PPIs, and (b) provide additional validation to currently annotated PPIs. The second goal is motivated by the desire to provide more levels of validation to the large number of complexes that were put onto Complex Portal through huMAP 3.0. A third goal, which may not get finished during the project period, is to leverage information about PPIs implicating proteins of unknown function to begin proposing new functions to them. 5. Proposed Activities 5a. Reanalysis on XL-MS data on PRIDE. As discussed above, there are 1,143 datasets on PRIDE that mention crosslinking, though only a small number (23) are considered “complete” submissions. This is because full submissions require processed data to be included as .mzIdentML file, which many crosslinking search software did not do till recently (because it wasn’t supported yet). 20 Moreover, many datasets are limited to technical studies on a few protein structures, often lacking biological relevance. We will compile an extended list of biologically meaningful, large-scale XL datasets for protein complex and PPI analysis (a preliminary list is included in the proposal as part of the Datasets Table). For each legacy submission, we will reannotate the dataset in SDRF with the sample metadata. Using the raw spectra, a fasta file, and user-inputted description containing essential information (like which crosslinker was used), we will reperform the search and validation using Scout 1.5 and then put these results back onto PRIDE under new PXD accessions as Complete submission in standard file format mzIdentML and a link to the original submission will be provided. After the resubmission, the data will be available in the novel PRIDE Crosslinking database (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pride/archive/crosslinking). This activity will be facilitated through the EMBL-EBI API for fetching many large raw data files. 5b. Conglomerate Pairwise Residue Interactions to Validate Predicted Complexes. For this aim, we will likely focus on a smaller, curated, subset of the ~1,00 reprocessed XL-MS accessions across multiple model organisms. The criteria for inclusion will be: (i) proteome-wide experimental design (whether it be in lysate or in-cell); (ii) use of MS-cleavable crosslinker (i.e., DSSO); (iii) experiments were in a model organism (i.e., yeast, HEK cells); (iv) scale of the submission is above some cut-off (i.e., >10 raw files). The total set of inter-protein crosslinks from these projects will be pooled together. We will be able to perform further analyses for human PPIs and yeast PPIs. For the human PPIs, we will first ask, are the two proteins in question associated with a complex in huMAP3.0 12 ? If so, we will perform an AlphaFold3 21 prediction on that protein pair and test if it predicts the two residues in the crosslinked residue-pair are close in the modeled interaction. If so, this will be taken as a higher level of validation for that pairwise interaction in the complex. The respective entry in the Complex Portal will be amended so that PPI edges that have this further structural support will be annotated as such; moreover, these PPI edges will also be labeled to include the detected residue-pairs between the two proteins and references to the relevant PRIDE accessions. A flowchart illustrating this activity is provided in Figure 2. This extra layer of validation for PPIs is a valuable contribution because 15,000 complexes in the human proteome does seem like an over-estimate, likely because AP-MS assays always have contaminants and bystander effects. XL- MS data, whilst not as high throughput, do represent a more direct form of evidence for a physical interaction between two proteins. For the PPIs that are not attested in huMAP3.0, we will also perform the AlphaFold3 prediction to see if the two residues are close in the modeled interaction. Those that pass this test will be added to Complex Portal under a provisional label that their evidence level is restricted to XL-MS. A similar cross-validation campaign can be executed for yeast, as Matthias Mann’s lab recently reported an interactome for yeast by performing 4,159 AP-MS (PRIDE PXD031940) experiments on (nearly) every protein in yeast. 22 If these objectives are completed earlier than expected, an additional activity we can set for ourselves is to reanalyze all AP-MS data on PRIDE Archive for organisms other than humans and yeast with quantms, 23 and then build a PPI network and cluster into complexes for each organism using the huMAP3.0 algorithm. This would then generate a list of complexes for a few non-yeast non-human model organism (likely Drosophila and mouse) that can also be compared to XL-MS data, following the same pipeline described above and in Figure 2. 5c. Propose Functions for Unannotated Proteins. According to one estimate, 15% of human proteins that can be assigned to orthogroups with other animal genes have unknown function (a “knownness score” of zero). 23 This is still a substantially large number of proteins (15% of 20,000 is 3,000). Many of these proteins likely do not contain catalytic activities themselves, since these are normally executed by globular catalytic domains that possess detectable levels of homology to known folds. However, a potentially common function for a protein of unknown function is to serve as a scaffold to bring other proteins together at a specific time and place. Hence, a great way to begin annotating these proteins is to see what PPIs they form. We propose to, in a limited form, apply this idea to the combined XL-MS dataset. For each validated PPI, we will assess its knownness score from the unknome. If one partner is 0, we will check if it interacts with a protein of known function. Examples of this will be compiled to see what patterns or network structures emerge. These data will likely be too sparse to merit updating any database of record with the findings; nevertheless, we hope the results can be published in some form and useful to create new hypotheses. 6. Outcomes 6a. Reanalysis on XL-MS data on PRIDE. The outcome of this activity will be recreation of ~100 large-scale different PRIDE submissions, reanalyzed in a standardized way and generating output in a standardised way, increasing the number of complete PRIDE crosslinking datasets from 23 (small datasets) to ~100 (biologically relevant large-scale submissions). This will facilitate re-use by enabling more users to view the residue-pair data without needing to be a mass spec expert or review the publications to find the residue-pairs in a large supplementary table. Moreover, it will make these data compatible for submissions to PDB-IHM if they are utilized for hybrid modeling.24 6b. Conglomerate Pairwise Residue Interactions to Validate Predicted Complexes. Complexes on Complex Portal that currently have low evidence levels will have their evidence levels increased if they are structurally consistent with crosslinks. Meanwhile new protein complexes will be proposed if identified crosslinks are consistent with a preliminary AI based structural prediction. We expect the efforts of the first two aims could be the subject of a high-impact publication. 6c. Propose Functions for Unannotated Proteins. If a few dozen proteins of unknown function (as described above) can be found with known interactors, we would use those examples as a starting point for future experiments and seek further (non-NCEMS) funding. 7. Working Group Approach The project requires deep familiarity with crosslinking mass spectrometry analysis, working with databases, structural biology, and data science. It would be rare to find all these expertise in a single research group. Dr. Fried’s team has a track-record on the structural biology and crosslinking mass spec side, but the EBI manages and runs PRIDE and Complex Portal, so Dr. Perez’s expertise and support are essential for automating the processes of retrieving, analyzing, and redepositing data onto these databases in a consistent high-throughput manner. Moreover, the primary work of activity a will involve a large amount of manual curation, and hence is not suitable for a graduate student or post-doc project; it is better accomplished by a trained data scientist. 8. Rationale for NCEMS Support Even though it is very rich with information, the complexities of XL-MS data processing and the lack of standardization in processed data output prevent it from being re-used and integrated. XL-MS data speak to both protein structure and interaction, and unlike other PPI detection methods, it is unique in its ability to test predictions about protein complex structures, now broadly available through AlphaFold3, which has also recently been made open source.25 Moreover, these modeling efforts are timely, as the RCSB transitions the PDB-dev to PDB-IHM (integrative and hybrid modeling) to highlight the greater importance of hybrid methods in structural biology. 9. Requested Resources Activity a will require 6 months of a data scientist’s FTE. This researcher will work closely with Dr. Perez and the EBI team. Hence, whilst they will be based at Penn State/NCEMS, we expect that they will benefit greatly from spending some time at EMBL-EBI in the United Kingdom for face-to-face interaction and cross-training, so some money for travel should be budgeted ($10k). To estimate the compute costs for data reanalysis, we offer the following approximation: (100 crosslinking PXDs)×(200 raw files/PXD on average)×(~1h Scout run/raw file), which is 20,000 h on a workstation that has 20 cores @ 5.0 GHz and 32 GB of memory. Activity b is in the realm of structural biology rather than data curation, and so the science can be done by a grad-student/post-doc in the Fried lab whose salary comes from another grant. This activity will be computationally expensive, as we estimate there will be ~10,000 AlphaFold3 calculations on pairs of proteins with average lengths of 500 residues. 10. Proposed Timeline 12-15 months total. Month 0-6 (activity a), project will be primarily driven by an NCEMS data scientist, advised by Dr. Perez- Riverol. Month 6-12 (activity b), project will be primarily driven by a Fried lab trainee, advised by Drs. Fried and Perez-Riverol. Month 12-15 (activity c), project is harder to define, but may involve a Fried lab trainee getting support from an NCEMS data scientist (in particular, with accessing data from the Unknome database).

proposals.proposal_title: Intelligent metadata compilation to enhance the reusability and discoverability of mass spectrometry-based proteomics data
proposals.abstract: Mass spectrometry-based proteomics generates vast amounts of data, yet the effective reuse and discovery of these datasets remain challenging due to incomplete and inconsistent metadata. Metadata, which provides critical contextual information such as experimental conditions, sample characteristics, and data processing details, is essential for making data FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable). To address these challenges, our working group aims to develop intelligent, automated workflows for comprehensive metadata extraction, harmonization, and integration into PRIDE, the largest public proteomics data repository. We will develop powerful bioinformatics and natural language processing tools to extract metadata directly from raw mass spectrometry files and scientific publications. By leveraging structured data standards, metadata will be enriched with controlled vocabulary terms, enhancing dataset transparency and usability. Community engagement through a machine-learning challenge will further drive innovation in metadata extraction techniques. The outcomes of the working group's activities will include automated metadata compilation workflows integrated into user-friendly tools, advanced dataset querying capabilities in PRIDE, and the creation of educational resources for the scientific community. These efforts will enable researchers to efficiently locate and reuse proteomics datasets, facilitating secondary analyses such as AI model training and large-scale reanalysis.
proposals.full_draft: Introduction and Goals In line with the FAIR principles1—findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable—omics data is increasingly accessible through public repositories tailored to diverse research domains. This surge in data availability has immense potential to accelerate scientific discovery and foster cross-disciplinary innovation. However, the effective findability and reusability (F and R in FAIR) of these datasets remain limited, primarily due to a lack of comprehensive metadata. Metadata, which includes details like experimental conditions, sample characteristics, data processing methods, and instrument settings, is critical for transforming raw data into scientifically valuable resources. Unfortunately, metadata is often incomplete, inconsistently structured, or buried in unstructured formats, such as free-form text in publications. These shortcomings restrict automated processing, systematic querying, and the discovery of relevant datasets. To bridge this gap, our working group will develop automated methods to extract, refine, and associate high-quality metadata with omics data in public repositories. This initiative will lay the groundwork for improved data discoverability and expanded reusability. While metadata enhancement is relevant across all omics fields, our initial focus is on mass spectrometry-based proteomics due to its complex metadata needs and established annotation frameworks. Specifically, we will leverage the SDRF-Proteomics format,2 which was recently adopted from transcriptomics (MAGE-TAB3) standards by the Proteomics Standards Initiative. 4 SDRF- Proteomics, a structured tab-delimited format, improves data transparency and usability by specifying clear relationships between samples, assays, and data files. However, despite a growing adoption since its introduction in 2021, fully annotated datasets remain limited, and many are inconsistently formatted,5 reducing their potential for reuse. Our working group proposes to address this gap by developing intelligent, automated workflows to systematically gather and associate metadata for proteomics experiments and integrate it into PRIDE,6 the largest proteomics data repository worldwide. Our tools will extract technical and biological metadata directly from experimental data, open access publications, and existing data annotations. Extracted metadata will be harmonized using controlled vocabulary/ontology terms and linked to datasets in PRIDE, creating an enriched metadata layer accessible to researchers for secondary analyses. To ensure accessibility and usability, we will implement a user-friendly interface within PRIDE’s web portal, alongside an online API for querying datasets based on metadata criteria. This integrated solution will empower researchers to efficiently locate, assess, and utilize proteomics data. Enhanced metadata infrastructure will unlock powerful capabilities for proteomics researchers. It will enable the identification of suitable training datasets for AI tools, such as spectrum prediction,7 de novo peptide sequencing,8 and repository-scale analysis tools.9 Additionally, metadata-enriched datasets will facilitate automated large-scale reanalyses, such as differential protein expression profiling across various biological conditions,10,11 empowering researchers to revisit and reinterpret public datasets in light of new hypotheses or improved methodologies. By enabling these and other advanced analyses, our approach will maximize the utility of proteomics data and pave the way for new scientific discoveries. Proposed Activities We will initially focus on non-specialized bottom-up discovery proteomics workflows, the most common application of mass spectrometry in proteomics, encompassing different experimental techniques such as data-dependent and data-independent acquisition with both label-free and label-based quantitation, as well as datasets enriched in post-translational modifications. Time permitting, we will expand to specialized proteomics approaches that synergize with other NCEMS initiatives, including crosslinking and hydrogen-deuterium exchange. This stepwise approach allows us to develop and validate our approaches in a controlled context while enabling adaptation to other omics disciplines in the future. Our metadata retrieval strategy will combine direct metadata extraction from raw mass spectrometry data and complementary metadata mining from scientific literature (Figure 1). From raw data, we will convert proprietary file formats to the open mzML standard 12 and derive essential experimental/technical metadata, such as instrument type and other parameters, and search parameters, including mass tolerances, digestion enzyme, and isobaric labeling strategies. To achieve this, we will leverage existing tools such as Param-Medic, which can infer mass tolerances13 and detect isobaric labeling.14 Additionally, organism identification will be derived by matching against known reference data,15 and details on digestion enzymes and post-translational modifications will be determined using open modification searching. 16 These Figure 1. Overview of the metadata compilation workflow. Automated workflows will extract metadata from mass spectrometry datasets and open-access publications using bioinformatics and text mining approaches. This functionality will be provided to users through tools, such as lesSDRF, and integrated into the PRIDE data repository, enhancing dataset discoverability and reusability. components will be integrated into an automated workflow using Nextflow 17 to streamline metadata extraction and organization. For literature-based metadata, we will gather critical contextual information not available in raw data, such as biological conditions, case/control groupings, and disease relevance. This will involve a natural language processing (NLP) pipeline utilizing large language models (LLMs) tailored for scientific text mining,18–20, trained and fine-tuned using open-access publications available in PubMed Central/Europe PMC. To ensure accuracy and avoid hallucinations, we will promote transparency and reliability in our results by configuring the LLM to indicate when metadata elements appear to be unavailable, include self-verification steps in LLM prompt chains,21 and experiment with using an LLM ensemble to check each others’ answers. To leverage broader expertise, we will launch a community machine-learning challenge—with which our team has prior experience22—focused on proteomics metadata extraction, offering token prizes to incentivize participation. Winning solutions will be licensed as open-source and integrated into our workflows. Additionally, we will make tutorial datasets and instructional resources available through ProteomicsML.23 This dual outreach to both data scientists and proteomics practitioners will ensure broad community engagement. To develop and validate our approach, we will use a curated set of 244 public datasets with SDRF metadata as a gold standard (December 2024; Data Source 1). Additionally, we will manually curate a private test set of up to 50 datasets (Data Source 2) to function as an independent benchmark for the machine-learning challenge and expand the available ground truth metadata for future validation efforts. Scoring of the metadata annotation results will emphasize precision over recall to ensure high-confidence metadata assignments and build trust in the system’s outputs. Finally, we will integrate our workflows into user-friendly tools like lesSDRF, 5 to automate metadata compilation during PRIDE submissions and allowing researchers to verify rather than manually input information. Retrospective metadata generation will be applied to existing public datasets with support from the PRIDE data curation team. Enhanced PRIDE functionality will include metadata-driven querying through their website and API-based dataset retrieval, empowering researchers to efficiently discover and reuse datasets. Outcomes 1. Automated metadata extraction workflows: Development of workflows to extract metadata from raw mass spectrometry files and from open-access manuscripts using NLP. 2. Community machine-learning challenge: Competition to generate innovative metadata extraction solutions, with winning algorithms open-sourced for broad use. 3. Educational resources on ProteomicsML: Tutorial datasets and documentation on ProteomicsML to engage and educate both data scientists and proteomics experts. 4. Enhanced metadata tools: Integration of the developed workflows into user-friendly tools like lesSDRF, enabling automated metadata generation during PRIDE submissions. 5. Advanced querying in PRIDE: Metadata-based querying functionality on PRIDE to find datasets and API support for programmatic dataset retrieval. 6. Academic contributions: A primary scientific manuscript detailing the complete metadata compilation system, as well as additional technical papers on specific aspects, such as NLP methodologies, community challenge outcomes, and workflow innovations. All project outputs will adhere to open science principles. Workflows and software solutions will be shared as open source under a permissive license via GitHub. Scientific manuscripts will be preprinted and published as open access, with associated data made publicly available upon preprint release or no later than official journal publication. While initially focused on mass spectrometry-based proteomics, these outcomes will serve as a template for addressing metadata challenges in other omics disciplines in the future, beginning with mass spectrometry-based metabolomics and extending to broader life sciences. Rationale for a Working Group Support Our team combines expertise in bioinformatics, machine learning, NLP, proteomics, and data repositories, enabling a comprehensive approach to metadata extraction and application that surpasses the capacity of individual research groups. Our machine learning and NLP experts will design and optimize algorithms to extract metadata from diverse sources, including raw mass spectrometry data files and scientific manuscripts. Our bioinformatics team will integrate these algorithms with structured data workflows to align metadata with established proteomics data standards. Proteomics specialists will ensure biological and analytical relevance, and community standards developers and data repository representatives will facilitate seamless integration with PRIDE. Rationale for NCEMS Support This project aligns with NCEMS’s mission to leverage publicly available data for large-scale synthesis, integrate diverse expertise, and develop innovative analytical strategies. NCEMS staff scientists and assistants will work alongside our team to curate SDRF metadata, support the community machine-learning challenge, and ensure effective workflow integration. CyVerse computational resources will provide the scalability and efficiency necessary to run NLP tasks and metadata extraction on repository-scale public data. The working group’s multidisciplinary nature will benefit from NCEMS’s leadership and team science training. Additional support for in-person collaboration will ensure that geographically distributed team members have dedicated opportunities to closely collaborate on tool integration. NCEMS’s project management support will also be important to ensure that the working group's efforts progress as planned and to coordinate the complex integration of newly developed tools with existing platforms and workflows. Furthermore, NCEMS’s contribution goes beyond providing technical and logistical support—it represents the vision to build and sustain multistakeholder initiatives that address important scientific challenges. Requested Resources NCEMS staff scientist and assistant support: Staff scientists and assistants with expertise in metadata harmonization, ideally with knowledge of proteomics experimental design, will contribute essential metadata curation activities. Staff scientists and assistants will support the NLP efforts by establishing and curating a corpus of open access scientific publications for text mining. Staff scientists will support community engagement efforts through technical management of the community machine-learning challenge. Staff scientists will provide technical guidance, assist in data analysis, and support the integration of workflows. To cover these activities, we request 33% FTE staff scientist and 50% staff scientist assistant FTE. Data storage and compute: ● 15 TB storage to mirror public proteomics data with existing SDRF metadata and newly annotated datasets. ● 2500 hours of CPU compute to extract technical metadata from mass spectrometry files using Nextflow pipelines. ● 500 hours of GPU compute to fine-tune and run locally-hosted LLMs (e.g., Ollama models) for extracting metadata from open access scientific publications. Proposed Timeline We request 2 years of NCEMS support according to the following anticipated timeline: Year 1: Development and initial testing ● Months 1–3: Kickoff meeting to establish roles, governance, and project workflow. Begin metadata compilation for public datasets to create the training and evaluation sets. ● Months 4–9: Develop initial workflows for (i) metadata extraction from raw mass spectrometry files and (ii) scientific manuscripts using NLP. ● Months 10–12: Implement and refine Nextflow pipelines for automated metadata extraction. Initial testing of workflows using existing curated datasets. ● Months 10–12: Launch community machine-learning challenge with prepared datasets and disseminate resources via ProteomicsML. Year 2: Evaluation, integration, and dissemination ● Months 13–15: Evaluate challenge solutions using private test datasets and incorporate winning algorithms. Start preparing scientific manuscripts on the methodologies and results. ● Months 16–18: Integrate workflows into lesSDRF for user-friendly metadata generation. Begin retrospective metadata generation for existing PRIDE datasets. ● Months 19–21: Provide metadata-based dataset querying functionality in PRIDE. ● Months 22–24: Finalize tools and manuscript publications.
